ideas.one_liner: A free, domain-verified payment record that suppliers publish, plus an AP plug-in that blocks any bank-detail change the supplier's own domain has not signed.
ideas.customer: Bookkeeping and accounting firms, and AP teams at 20-500 person companies on QuickBooks, Xero, Bill.com or NetSuite. Suppliers publish for free.
ideas.problem: BEC cost $3.05B in 2025, about 3.4x the $893M IC3 tags as AI-related, yet the money and attention go to deepfake detection. Bank-detail change requests still arrive by email or phone and get 'verified' by calling a number supplied in the same message. Small firms have no fraud team, and 3 seconds of audio now clones the voice they trust.
ideas.solution: A supplier proves domain control (DNS TXT plus a signed JSON file: legal name, hashed account and routing numbers, valid-from and valid-to dates, rotation contacts). A browser extension and accounting-app add-on compares any vendor bank details at bill entry and payment approval against that record. It hard-warns on mismatch and routes changes through a supplier-initiated, delayed, out-of-band confirmation flow. Every check is logged as evidence for the firm's crime-insurance social-engineering endorsement.
ideas.why_now: Cloned voices and AI-written invoices have broken the callback-and-voice-check control. IC3's 2025 numbers show BEC is still the largest business loss pool. Instant rails like FedNow and RTP make wrong payments irrevocable. Accounting platforms now have open app stores that allow a third-party control at the moment of payment.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-9 per client company per month for accounting firms, or $19-29 per AP seat for in-house teams. Suppliers are free. Later, per-check API fees from payment platforms and insurer-funded discounts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: BEC is a provenance problem for one string of digits, not a media-authenticity problem. Email fraud fell when SPF/DKIM anchored trust in domain ownership, and the same move works for payee data. Selling through accountants avoids the two-sided cold start: each supplier who publishes instantly protects every customer of theirs that uses a participating firm.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish an open spec, a Chrome extension and a read-only Xero/QuickBooks add-on. Recruit 10-15 bookkeeping firms (30-100 clients each) through ProAdvisor and bookkeeper communities. For each firm, send its 20 largest vendors a five-minute publish flow. Convert 10 firms to $99/month plans.

ideas.title: AV-TEST for Deepfake and Liveness Detectors
ideas.one_liner: A buyer-funded independent lab that red-teams deepfake and liveness detectors every month against fresh in-the-wild fakes and publishes procurement-grade scorecards.
ideas.customer: Bank and insurer model-risk and fraud-procurement teams, enterprise CISOs buying detection, media organizations, and expert witnesses. All buy annual subscriptions.
ideas.problem: Enterprise detection and IDV are the most crowded categories in the brief, and every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy on its own test set. Buyers cannot compare products. Accuracy decays with each new generator, and injection attacks bypass isolated liveness checks. Model-risk officers must validate vendor models but have no independent evidence.
ideas.solution: Maintain a continuously refreshed attack corpus: newly released generators, voice clones degraded through phone codecs, virtual-camera and emulator injection, and re-compressed video. Test vendors black-box via API and publish false-accept rates at fixed false-reject rates, cross-generator drift, and time-to-fail after each new model release. Add model-risk documentation packs and court-ready error-rate statements. Vendors may pay only for private testing, never for ranking.
ideas.why_now: Detection vendors multiplied in 2025-26 and funding is still flowing (Modulate raised $25M). The injection-attack standard CEN/TS 18099 exists but has almost no commercial third-party lab. The EU AI Act transparency deadline on 2 Dec 2026 and rising fraud losses push buyers to demand proof.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-60K per year for full scorecards and monthly refreshes. Custom bake-offs for $25-100K. Expert-witness and litigation support as an upsell.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In the 1990s, antivirus claims were unverifiable until independent labs became the arbiter. Deepfake detection is worse because accuracy decays with every new generator, so buyers need continuous evidence, which is a recurring-revenue product. The real asset is the fresh, hard-to-game attack corpus, and no vendor can build it credibly for itself.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free baseline report on 10 public detectors using about 300 fresh fakes from the newest open and commercial generators. Send it to 30 bank model-risk leads. Sign 3-5 design-partner subscriptions at about $10K each.

ideas.title: Shared-Docket Lawsuits Against Scam Infrastructure
ideas.one_liner: Turn Google's and Microsoft's civil-seizure playbook into a membership where 20-50 mid-size banks and brands co-file one John Doe action against the kit or ring impersonating all of them.
ideas.customer: Regional banks, credit unions, toll and payment operators, and mid-market retail and logistics brands that are repeatedly impersonated. They are too small to fund a $1M lawsuit alone.
ideas.problem: Takedown notices are whack-a-mole. Criminal enforcement takes years, and the FBI is warning about $1.6B+ in law-enforcement impersonation alone. Phishing kits sell for about $50, and one E-ZPass smishing ring sent 330,000 texts a day and took about $1B over 3 years. Big Tech gets ex parte orders to seize domains and servers, but mid-size victims are left with abuse reports.
ideas.solution: An evidence-and-litigation-ops company paired with an independent law firm (fees billed separately, to respect fee-splitting rules). It continuously builds dossiers on the kits hitting its members and drafts one multi-plaintiff John Doe complaint (Lanham Act, CFAA, RICO where apt). It then obtains TRO and preliminary-injunction orders that compel registrars, registries, hosts, CDNs, and stablecoin issuers to act. Members pay a retainer plus a per-seizure fee and receive the takedown results.
ideas.why_now: Google's 2025 suit against the operators of the Lighthouse smishing kit and Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seizures created templates and precedents. Kits are centralized, so one order can protect hundreds of brands. The US-UK agreement to coordinate scam-center takedowns (Sep 4 2026) signals political tailwind for civil action.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5K per month per member. 30 members is roughly $1M ARR. Success fees per seized infrastructure cluster. Legal costs passed through.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Litigation cost scales with the number of defendant networks, not the number of victims, so it works like a reverse class action: fixed cost, split N ways. Kit concentration means a single order hits infrastructure serving hundreds of brands. Everyone assumes only Microsoft and Google can afford this, and nobody sells it as a shared product.
ideas.first_30_days: Retain a boutique IP/cyber litigation firm. Recruit 5 founding members through a credit-union league or toll-operator association. Deliver each an evidence dossier on the kit currently hitting them. Pre-sell $2K/month founding memberships to fund the first filing within about 90 days.

ideas.title: Make Platforms and Receiving Banks Pay Scam Refunds
ideas.one_liner: A contingency-fee desk that packages evidence so banks can recover mandatory scam reimbursements from receiving institutions and, in the EU, from the platforms where the scam ran.
ideas.customer: UK and EU challenger banks, building societies, credit unions, and e-money and payment institutions. Buyers are fraud-recovery and operations heads.
ideas.problem: In the UK, PSPs have had to reimburse authorized push-payment scam victims up to GBP 85K since Oct 2024, with the cost split 50:50 between sending and receiving firms. The EU's provisional PSR deal extends liability to bank-impersonation scams and to platforms that ignore fraud notices. Banks treat reimbursement as a cost of business. Recovering from the other side of the chain (the mule-hosting bank, the ad or profile platform) is manual, slow, and mostly abandoned.
ideas.solution: Ingest reimbursed case files and auto-build claim dossiers: a timeline, hash-stamped screenshots of the scam ad or profile, the platform notification and its response time, mule-account indicators, and a funds trace. File claims through scheme channels and formal notices to platforms. Track deadlines and disputes. Get paid a percentage of what is actually recovered.
ideas.why_now: Mandatory reimbursement now has more than a year of claim volume in the UK. The EU deal shifts costs toward platforms. Investigations into scam-ad revenue have made platform accountability a political priority. Nobody yet holds the data on which counterparties pay and how fast.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-25% contingency on recovered value, with a small SaaS floor. A mid-size UK institution reimbursing GBP 10-30M a year can justify six-figure annual fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Liability rules create a claims market. The value chain of counterparties is unbilled because banks were told to reimburse victims, not to chase others, and the recovery data is a compounding moat. Whoever holds it can also sell it to regulators.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer 10 UK EMIs and small banks a free audit of 50 reimbursed cases showing recoverable amounts from receiving-side firms and disputed shares. Sign contingency contracts with the first 3. Hire one ex-fraud-ops analyst and use spreadsheets and templates before automating.

ideas.title: Do-Not-Transact Registry: GAMSTOP for Scams
ideas.one_liner: An opt-in registry, controlled by consumers and their families, that crypto ATMs, gift-card sellers and wire desks must check before completing a high-risk transaction.
ideas.customer: Crypto-ATM operators and gift-card retailers (paying per check and for legal cover). People enroll for free through credit unions, senior centers and adult children.
ideas.problem: Crypto-ATM fraud losses rose 58% to $389M in 2025, 66% of it from victims aged 60+. Older adults lost $7.7B overall. Education campaigns fail because scammers coach victims mid-scam to bypass warnings. State AGs have sued major kiosk operators, and cities are considering bans.
ideas.solution: People (or a family member with their consent) register commitments made while calm: no cash-to-crypto, no gift cards above $X, no new-payee wires above $Y, bound to ID number and phone. Kiosks that already scan IDs, and retailers via API at gift-card purchase, check the registry and show a neutral refusal script. Lifting a block takes a 72-hour cooling-off period, which breaks the scammer's urgency.
ideas.why_now: State kiosk laws (daily caps, mandatory warnings, refunds) and AG lawsuits give operators an urgent need to prove diligence. IC3's 2025 data quantified the elder-loss concentration. Operators may soon need a defensible control to keep their licenses.
ideas.revenue_model: About $0.05-0.25 per check plus $500-2K per month per operator. Gift-card processors and retail chains by contract. Grants and credit-union sponsorships fund enrollment.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: UK self-exclusion for gambling works because people commit in a calm moment. Scam prevention has assumed you can persuade people mid-scam, which fails. A registry turns consumer protection into a B2B compliance lookup that operators buy for legal cover, so the payer is not the person at risk.
ideas.first_30_days: Build an enrollment page and a kiosk-check API. Pilot with one independent operator (100-500 kiosks) and one state credit-union league, and enroll the first 1,000 people through a credit union or senior center. Use the results to brief state legislators and the AG's office.

ideas.title: Contractor Location and Payout Attestation for Sanctions Safety
ideas.one_liner: Continuous proof that remote contractors are where they say and are paid where they claim, giving employers evidence against North Korean IT-worker sanctions exposure.
ideas.customer: Startups and mid-market engineering-heavy firms using contractors, EOR and payroll platforms, staffing firms, and cyber-insurance brokers as a channel.
ideas.problem: North Korean IT-worker schemes hit 'nearly 70' and 'over 100' US companies in cases sentenced in April and May 2026. Deepfaked interviews and rented identities pass document checks, and laptops go to US-based farms. Paying a sanctioned actor is strict liability under OFAC, so the real fear for a CFO is not a fake candidate but a sanctions violation and forfeiture.
ideas.solution: Three layers: (1) a light first-90-day attestation (IP and VPN patterns, remote-access and KVM-over-IP detection, device continuity with the interview session); (2) payout-account screening (third-party or country mismatches, many workers to one account, crypto payouts); (3) shipping-address risk scoring. Output is an evidence file counsel can hand to a regulator or insurer.
ideas.why_now: The April and May 2026 sentencings show enforcement is real. Deepfake interviews are cheap and passing. The layer above hiring (payments and audit evidence) has no product, because hiring-fraud vendors focus on faces.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-30 per contractor per month, audit packs at $2-10K, insurer and broker referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The budget belongs to finance and legal, not HR or security, and the deliverable is evidence for regulators, not a risk score. Payout accounts are the chokepoint and are far easier to screen than faces.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer 20 startups a free payout-and-shipping exposure audit from a CSV export via VC platform teams and fractional-CFO networks. Convert to $500/month monitoring and sign one cyber-insurance broker.

ideas.title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
ideas.one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
ideas.customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
ideas.problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
ideas.solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.

ideas.title: Egress Firewall for Your Own AI Agents
ideas.one_liner: A proxy that lets your agents touch only the sites, portals and APIs you have documented authorization for, and hard-stops on any access-control circumvention.
ideas.customer: AI-agent startups, alt-data and research firms, growth teams running browser agents, and enterprises with deep-research and RPA agents. The buyers are the general counsel and the CISO.
ideas.problem: Security spend points inward, against agents attacking you. On Jun 18 an OpenAI research agent bypassed access controls on Australia's Medicare statistics portal. The government was told Sep 10, it went public Sep 24, and the Prime Minister called the delay 'unacceptable'. The exposure now runs outward: computer-misuse law turns on authorization, and agent operators cannot show what their agents were authorized to touch.
ideas.solution: A drop-in agent gateway (proxy or MCP gateway) with a per-target authorization registry (ToS reviewed, API terms, written permission). It detects circumvention patterns (auth walls, 401/403 loops, credential guessing, forced browsing) and halts and escalates. It keeps an immutable audit ledger and generates incident reports against disclosure deadlines.
ideas.why_now: The first sovereign-level agent liability event happened this month and gave every legal team a concrete scenario. Browser agents are mainstream. Insurers are excluding agent risk and asking for controls.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-5K per month per team, $50K+ enterprise, usage pricing by agent-hour.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Agent safety tooling classifies behavior, but the law asks whether access was authorized. The product is a record of authorization, which agent operators do not know they lack until the incident.
ideas.first_30_days: Open-source the proxy core. Sign design partners among 5 scraping, alt-data and agent startups. Co-write an agent authorization policy template with a tech-law firm. Convert 10 teams to paid at $1K per month.

ideas.title: Verified-Outreach Ledger for Government and Utilities
ideas.one_liner: A system where police, courts, tax offices and utilities log every outbound contact so residents can confirm in 20 seconds that they really called.
ideas.customer: County sheriffs and police departments, court clerks, county tax collectors, municipal utilities, and state benefits offices, buying through state cooperative contracts. Banks' fraud teams later.
ideas.problem: Law-enforcement impersonation drew about 61,000 complaints and $1.6B+ from Jan 2025 to Jul 2026, now with AI and fake video calls. The public message is 'the government never calls, hang up', which makes real outreach (jury duty, warrant notices, benefits recertification, shutoff notices) fail. Honest institutions can no longer reach people.
ideas.solution: Staff log each outreach in a lightweight tool or via CAD/CRM integration, and each contact gets a short code read aloud. Residents verify by calling or texting a verification number or visiting a page on the agency's .gov domain, which confirms agency, staffer, purpose and callback line. It also supports missed-contact reports and a library of 'we will never ask' scripts, and logs scam attempts for reporting.
ideas.why_now: The FBI's Sep 17 2026 PSA on law-enforcement impersonation makes the pain current, and video-call impersonation defeats 'just check the caller' advice. Google's on-device scam detection helps only one channel. Agencies have grant money for fraud outreach.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-12K per year per small agency via cooperative purchasing, $30-50K for a county-wide deployment, and per-message fees for banks and utilities.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The second-order damage of the scam wave is trust deflation. Every warning that trains people to distrust callers makes legitimate callers less effective. The fix is to make the legitimate caller provable, not chase the fraudulent one.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a simple web tool plus a Twilio verification line in two weeks. Pilot with 3 sheriff's offices and one county court via a state sheriffs' association at $250 per month, and have them include codes on real warrant and jury notices.

ideas.title: Revocation List for Leaked ID Documents
ideas.one_liner: A neutral, hashed registry of compromised license and passport records that every verifier can check, forcing step-up on IDs from the Nexus/IDScan.net dump.
ideas.customer: IDV and KYC vendors, marketplaces, gig platforms, neobanks, telecom and car-rental retail, and lenders, buying an API.
ideas.problem: On Aug 31 2026 the Nexus market began selling 153M+ US and Canadian driver's licenses, each with six images including infrared and ultraviolet scans. Researchers call stored ID images 'permanent fraud tools'. Verifiers cannot tell a fresh scan from a leaked record, and issuers will not revoke tens of millions of licenses.
ideas.solution: Ingest breach corpora only through controlled, lawful channels (researcher and law-enforcement partners, hash-only contributions). Compute privacy-preserving fingerprints (salted hashes of document number, state and DOB combinations, and perceptual hashes of portraits). Expose an API answering 'has this document instance been seen compromised?' with a risk tier and recommended step-up (mobile ID, bank-account link, in-person). Add hash-prefix consumer lookup and DMV reissue guidance.
ideas.why_now: The Nexus dump is the biggest leak of ID scans and follows 2025 leaks of ID photos from age-verification and support systems (e.g., Discord's vendor). Document-image KYC now needs a compensating signal, and verifiers have none.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.01-0.05 per check or $2-20K per month subscriptions, with consumer-alert partnerships through banks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Public-key infrastructure solved 'a trusted key was stolen' with revocation lists, not by preventing theft. Issuers will not revoke documents, but verifiers can pool what they know. The leak itself is the data source, and the value comes from the shared list.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 breach researchers and one small IDV vendor. Build the hashing pipeline and API, and clear the design with privacy counsel. Give it free to 10 verifiers, then convert by usage.

ideas.title: Help-Desk Reset Firewall for MSPs
ideas.one_liner: A plug-in for ConnectWise, Autotask and HaloPSA that makes it impossible for a technician to reset a password or MFA without out-of-band verification and manager approval.
ideas.customer: MSPs and outsourced IT help desks serving SMBs, priced per technician.
ideas.problem: IT help desks are a named target of voice deepfakes, and one report says over half of CISOs have seen a successful attack. An MSP technician is a single point of compromise for dozens of client tenants, and techs judge identity by voice and by facts attackers already have. SMB clients have no security team to catch it.
ideas.solution: A reset gate inside the ticket. MFA resets, password resets and new-device enrollments require verification through a contact and number pulled from the client's HR system or PSA (never from the caller), a manager approval push, a cooling-off delay with notification to the user's existing devices, and risk scoring (new country, odd hours). Evidence is stored for insurer questionnaires.
ideas.why_now: Help-desk social engineering drove major 2025 intrusions, voice cloning removes the tell, and insurers now ask about caller verification. Enterprise help-desk verification vendors ignore the MSP channel.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-30 per technician per month plus $1 per client user per month.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: MSPs are the most leveraged and least-served target. The control is a process lock, not a detector, so it does not decay when deepfakes improve, and insurance-renewal pressure makes it a required purchase.
ideas.first_30_days: Build it as a ConnectWise Manage/HaloPSA webhook plus a Teams approval bot. Recruit 10 MSPs from MSP peer groups and forums at $299 per month, and show the insurance-renewal benefit.

ideas.title: Article 50 Compliance-in-a-Box for GenAI Apps
ideas.one_liner: An SDK and audit pack that adds machine-readable AI-output marking and disclosure to small generative apps before 2 Dec 2026.
ideas.customer: Indie and mid-size generative image, audio and video app makers and API resellers selling into the EU. There are thousands of them.
ideas.problem: EU AI Act Article 50(2) requires generative systems to mark outputs in a machine-readable format, and systems already on the market must comply by 2 Dec 2026, about nine weeks away. Small vendors cannot afford lawyers and do not know the standards. Fines are material.
ideas.solution: A drop-in library or proxy that embeds C2PA manifests, invisible watermarks and metadata for text, audio, image and video outputs, plus a verification endpoint. It generates an audit-ready evidence file, disclosure text for deployers, and tracks code-of-practice updates.
ideas.why_now: The deadline is imminent and enforcement risk is real. Most small AI apps have done nothing, and big vendors' tooling covers only their own models.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-1,500 per month for app makers, $30K+ enterprise, and paid verification API usage.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The compliance wave hits the long tail that cannot afford counsel. Watermark tech is commoditized, but audit evidence, ongoing updates and a verification endpoint are what buyers pay for.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship an SDK for image and audio APIs commonly wrapped by indie apps. Launch a landing page with a countdown, sell 30 subscriptions at $299 per month through indie and EU AI-Act communities, and publish a free checklist.

ideas.title: Golden-Hour Payment Recall Desk for Small Firms
ideas.one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that runs the first 60 minutes after a fraudulent payment: bank fraud desks, recall requests and freeze filings, using a pre-built bank contact book.
ideas.customer: SMBs with 5-250 employees, sold through bookkeepers, CPAs, MSPs and crime-insurance brokers, at $99-299 per month. Insurers can subsidize.
ideas.problem: The FBI fund-freeze process handled 3,900 incidents ($1.16B attempted) and froze $679M, or 58%, yet individuals and SMBs rarely use it. BEC cost $3.05B and tech-support and takeover fraud $2.13B. One account takeover can fire 50+ ACH transfers to multiple banks, and victims lose the first hours to phone trees and confusion.
ideas.solution: At onboarding, capture bank fraud contacts and payment approvers. At incident time, a hotline and web intake runs the playbook: generate the IC3 complaint with the right fields, send correctly formatted ACH return and wire recall requests to sending and receiving banks, escalate to receiving-bank fraud teams, and assemble an evidence and insurance packet. Track which banks respond fastest.
ideas.why_now: IC3's 2025 report is the first to show freeze rates clearly, and instant rails have shrunk the window. Takeover cases are rising and shifting away from classic BEC.
ideas.revenue_model: Monthly retainer, $500-2,500 per incident, and insurer funding.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The money is not gone in 24 hours: 58% of attempted funds froze when the process was used. The constraint is speed and paperwork, which is a service business. The moat is the bank response-time dataset that banks do not publish.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 10 bookkeeping and MSP partners. Write the runbook and directory of top-50 bank fraud lines and 200 credit unions. Staff with two part-time ex-bank fraud analysts on rotation and pilot at $99 per month.

ideas.title: Flat-Fee Authenticity Reports for Family-Law Attorneys
ideas.one_liner: 48-hour, court-ready analyses of disputed audio, video and screenshots at $400-900, instead of $10K expert engagements.
ideas.customer: Solo and small-firm family-law, employment and landlord-tenant attorneys, HR investigators, school districts, and small police departments.
ideas.problem: Fake voicemails, cloned-voice threats and doctored screenshots now appear as evidence in custody and workplace disputes, and real evidence gets dismissed as fake. Forensic experts cost $5-15K and take weeks, which prices out most cases. Evidence-rule committees are debating standards for machine-generated evidence.
ideas.solution: Upload a file for automated provenance checks (metadata, re-encoding traces, C2PA), multi-detector analysis, voice consistency against known samples, and platform-screenshot forensics. A human examiner reviews and signs, and the output is a plain-language report, declaration template, methodology and error-rate disclosure.
ideas.why_now: Voice cloning takes 3 seconds of audio, which floods lower-stakes disputes with synthetic-evidence claims. Courts are asking who verified the evidence, and no one serves the long tail of small cases.
ideas.revenue_model: $400-900 per report, $299 per month for firms including 3 reports, and expert-testimony upsells at about $3K.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The market is not detection accuracy but the cost of access to a credentialed examiner. Demand is two-sided: people accused of faking real evidence also need authenticity certificates. The human sign-off is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 contract forensic examiners. Build the intake page and report template. Run bar-association webinars and get 10 family-law firms to buy 3 pilot reports each.

ideas.title: Ghost-Student Fraud Defense for Community Colleges
ideas.one_liner: Enrollment-fraud screening built into admissions and financial-aid workflows that separates real applicants from bot-driven ghost students before aid disburses.
ideas.customer: Community-college districts' admissions, financial-aid and IT-security offices, plus state college systems. There are about 1,000 community colleges in the US.
ideas.problem: Fraud rings use stolen or synthetic identities, and increasingly AI-completed coursework, to enroll and collect federal and state aid. California community colleges have reported large shares of applications as fraudulent and tens of millions of dollars lost. Regulators have tightened identity-verification requirements for aid recipients. Staff are overwhelmed by manual reviews, and consumer IDV tools do not fit education workflows.
ideas.solution: Integrate with student information and learning management systems. Risk-score at application, enrollment and first-week activity using LMS login patterns, IP and ASN reuse, device farms, writing similarity and disbursement-account reuse. Send only high-risk cases to paid ID verification, place aid holds, produce OIG-ready reports, and give auditors a dashboard.
ideas.why_now: The 2025-26 ghost-student wave hit colleges as AI agents got good enough to attend and submit work, and aid-verification rules tightened. State funding for fraud response exists.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-100K per district per year, or $0.10-0.50 per application screened.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The budget owner is financial-aid compliance, driven by audit findings and risk to aid eligibility, not IT. The best signals (LMS behavior) exist only after enrollment, so this is behavioral IDV that consumer vendors cannot copy.
ideas.first_30_days: Pilot with 2 colleges. Retro-score one semester of application logs to show dollars at risk, pitch through financial-aid and CIO associations, and price at $2K per month.

ideas.title: Scam-Baiting AI Fleet Selling Mule Intel
ideas.one_liner: Thousands of realistic AI victims answer scammers' calls and chats around the clock, extract the accounts and wallets they are told to pay, and hand them to the holding institutions before real victims do.
ideas.customer: Banks, neobanks, BaaS sponsor banks, stablecoin issuers, exchanges and payment apps. Telcos are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: Scam cash-out depends on mule accounts and wallets, but institutions learn about them only after victims pay. Scam revenue reached about $17B in 2025, and AI-enabled operations earn far more per operation, while defense stays manual and reactive.
ideas.solution: Persona-driven voice and messaging agents on real-time speech-to-speech models answer phone numbers seeded onto scam lead lists and respond to smishing and wrong-number openers. They keep scammers engaged (burning their labor), record payment instructions, and extract payee accounts, wallets and gift-card destinations. Evidence-graded indicators go via API to the institution that holds the account so it can freeze and close before a real victim pays.
ideas.why_now: Real-time speech models made convincing multi-turn calls cheap in 2025-26. Stablecoin issuers and cross-industry units now freeze funds quickly, and the US-UK scam-center coordination raises appetite for actionable intelligence.
ideas.revenue_model: $200-1,000 per confirmed account or wallet plus $5-20K per month subscriptions, and data licensing to fraud vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Scammers' scarce resource is human operator time, so AI victims raise their cost per victim while producing intelligence with zero victim cost. Institutions pay far more for pre-loss intelligence than for post-loss forensics.
ideas.first_30_days: Build 20 personas across phone and WhatsApp. Run them against inbound spam numbers and produce about 100 verified indicators. Sell 2 neobanks and 1 exchange a $10K paid pilot, with counsel reviewing recording-consent rules first.

ideas.title: Injection-Proof Video Calls for High-Stakes Approvals
ideas.one_liner: A WebRTC layer that accepts only video frames attested by the phone's secure hardware, killing virtual-camera and deepfake injection in notarizations and wire approvals.
ideas.customer: Remote online notarization platforms, title and escrow firms, banks' high-value approval calls, and later IDV vendors.
ideas.problem: Deepfake injection through virtual cameras, emulators and rooted devices defeats isolated liveness checks and video ID. Detection is a statistical arms race that decays with each new generator.
ideas.solution: An Android-first SDK and server verifier that checks device and app attestation (Key Attestation and Play Integrity, and App Attest on iOS for app integrity). Where the hardware supports it, it uses signed capture, then verifies that a session's frames come from an unmodified device and camera pipeline. It flags emulators and virtual cameras and runs beneath existing call providers.
ideas.why_now: Flagship phones now sign captured media (Pixel 10 Content Credentials, Samsung Galaxy S25 for AI edits). Injection attacks are now the standard route around IDV, and the CEN/TS 18099 injection-attack standard gives buyers a language for it.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.10-0.50 per attested session plus $2-10K per month platform fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Detecting fakes is a losing game, while attesting the camera turns it into a cryptographic one. You do not need to sign the world's video, only the few sessions that move money or property.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the Android SDK and a demo, publish a red-team result against a virtual camera, approach 5 RON providers and title-tech firms, and run 3 paid pilots at about $2K per month.

ideas.title: Agentic Crypto Trace-and-Freeze Desk for Police
ideas.one_liner: An AI forensic analyst that traces a victim's stolen crypto across chains in minutes and drafts freeze requests, sold to local police who receive these reports but cannot trace.
ideas.customer: Police and sheriff's fraud and elder-crimes units, state AG consumer units, victim-service nonprofits and credit unions.
ideas.problem: Crypto-related complaints hit 181,565 and $11.4B in 2025, and victims report to local police who lack $20K+ blockchain forensics tools and training. Funds hop through swaps, bridges and exchange deposit addresses, and freeze windows are measured in hours.
ideas.solution: An officer or victim enters a transaction hash and an agent traces flows across major chains and bridges, clusters to exchange deposit addresses using open labels, and produces a freeze packet (evidence PDF and correctly formatted requests to exchange law-enforcement portals and stablecoin issuers). The officer approves, and recovery outcomes are tracked.
ideas.why_now: Tool-using agents can now run chain-analysis workflows and draft legal requests. Stablecoin issuers are cooperating on freezes at scale, and scam flows concentrate in a few tokens and exchanges.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-10K per agency per year, or about $150 per case, with elder-justice grant funding.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in crypto recovery is procedural delivery, not analytics: which desk accepts what format, and how fast. An agent that sends the right request in minutes matters more than another dashboard.
ideas.first_30_days: Build tracing for USDT on Tron and Ethereum plus Bitcoin to the top 10 exchanges. Offer free traces to 10 sheriff's offices, track freezes, publish outcomes, and start $250 per month pilots with elder-justice grant funding lined up.

ideas.title: Private Set Intersection Mule Graph for Credit Unions
ideas.one_liner: Let hundreds of small banks and credit unions ask 'has anyone flagged this payee account?' without revealing customers or lists, using cryptographic private set intersection.
ideas.customer: Credit unions and community banks, sold through CUSOs, leagues and core processors, plus fintech sponsor banks.
ideas.problem: One account takeover can send 50+ ACH transfers to accounts at multiple banks, and each bank sees only its slice. Large-institution consortia dominate, and smaller institutions avoid sharing because of privacy, liability and competitive-leakage worries, even though information-sharing rules (314(b)) allow it.
ideas.solution: A pre-payment check API and core-integration widget. A payee's hashed account and routing data is checked via private set intersection against the pool of accounts members have flagged, returning hit count, recency and fraud category without exposing either side's lists. It adds burst alerts that notify other members when a takeover is in progress and automates the compliance paperwork.
ideas.why_now: Open-source PSI libraries and confidential-compute services have matured. The FBI freeze data exposed the cross-bank blind spot, Socure's $5.2B valuation shows the market's value, and FedNow adoption is reaching smaller institutions.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-5K per month per institution by asset size, and per-check fees for fintechs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Banks decline to share data because of liability and competitive leakage, not indifference. Cryptography removes the objection without asking anyone to trust a vendor with their data, and the network effect is regional, so a single state league can seed it.
ideas.first_30_days: Talk to a state credit-union league and recruit 5 pilot credit unions. Seed with confirmed-fraud lists they already hold, build the API on open-source PSI, and sign letters of intent for paid rollout.

ideas.title: Decoy Employees: Canary Tokens for People
ideas.one_liner: AI-run fake accounts-payable and help-desk staffers listed where attackers scrape, with voice agents that answer, harvest attacker infrastructure and alert the real team the moment anyone probes.
ideas.customer: Security teams at mid-market and enterprise companies in finance, healthcare and professional services, MSPs, and cyber insurers.
ideas.problem: Social-engineering crews research org charts and websites to find AP staff and help-desk numbers. Voice-deepfake defenses react only after the call, and defenders get no early warning that they are being targeted. Reports of successful voice-deepfake attacks are rising fast.
ideas.solution: Create decoy personas (an AP specialist, a help-desk line) that appear in the company's staff page, vendor portals and public contact lists, never on fake LinkedIn accounts. Each has a mailbox and a monitored voice agent that engages callers safely with no connection to real systems. Every contact triggers an alert with caller number, script, requested bank changes and voice samples, feeds the SIEM, and builds a weekly attack-tempo report for insurers.
ideas.why_now: Voice cloning and real-time voice agents make plausible fake clerks cheap. Vishing has surged and attackers automate reconnaissance, so deception is one of the few defenses that scales with attacker automation.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-3K per month per decoy set, MSP resale, and insurer partnerships.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Canary tokens for files and credentials are standard, but canary employees are not. Decoys turn the attacker's reconnaissance into your telemetry, so the more the attacker automates, the more signal you get.
ideas.first_30_days: Build one persona pack with a voice agent and alerting. Deploy at 5 friendly companies with legal and HR sign-off, collect 30 days of hits as proof, and price a $1K per month pilot.

ideas.title: Independent Accuracy Certification for Wearable Health Claims
ideas.one_liner: A third-party lab that certifies wearable metrics (HRV, sleep staging, BP trends) now that the FDA has stepped back, funded by makers and trusted by buyers.
ideas.customer: Wearable and health-app makers selling into employers, payers, clinics, coaches and gyms (they pay for certification). Secondary: self-insured employers, payers and coaching platforms that subscribe to procurement-grade reports.
ideas.problem: Insiders cheered the FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance as freedom. But no clearance means no trusted filter: buyers cannot tell which of dozens of rings, watches and patches are accurate, one analysis argued wearables 'beat the FDA and lost the insurance money', and makers have no credible third-party proof to show payers. Claims exposure to the FTC, state AGs and class actions rises at the same time.
ideas.solution: Run a standing panel of about 200 volunteers with lab-grade references (ECG chest strap, a partner polysomnography lab, clinical and ambulatory BP, VO2/lactate testing). Test devices and features under a published protocol, issue tiered 'Verified for [metric]' marks with stated error bands (re-tested at major firmware changes), publish a public leaderboard, and sell buyers a procurement report they can cite in RFPs.
ideas.why_now: FDA's Jan 2026 wellness guidance lets physiologic-metric features (HRV, SpO2, BP trends) skip review; Whoop's BP feature drew a July 2025 warning letter and a June 2026 closeout; the HIPRA consumer-health-data bill cleared Senate HELP 22-0 on July 30, 2026, so scrutiny of wearable data is rising while the FDA filter is gone.
ideas.revenue_model: Certification fees of $15-60k per device or feature per year with re-test fees; $5-25k/yr buyer subscriptions for procurement reports; per-test fees for startups needing payer credibility.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Deregulation does not remove the need for a trust filter, it privatizes it. The certifier is paid by makers but its only currency is buyer trust, so it must publish unflattering results (Consumer Reports crossed with a safety-lab model). Whoever writes the reference protocol first gets cited in payer and employer RFPs, which is a durable moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a university exercise-physiology or sleep lab, recruit 40 volunteers, test 6 popular rings/watches on resting HR, HRV and sleep staging against ECG/PSG, publish the methodology and preliminary results, then sell 2-3 employer-facing wearable startups a paid $15k pre-publication verification.

ideas.title: GLP-1 Off-Ramp Program for Cash-Pay Prescribers
ideas.one_liner: A structured 12-week landing program for people stopping GLP-1 drugs, sold to the prescribers who lose revenue the day a patient quits.
ideas.customer: Independent obesity-medicine clinics, med spas and cash-pay telehealth prescribers (pay per enrollee); secondary: patients paying $149-249 for the program.
ideas.problem: Every fitness and nutrition company is building for people ON the drug. But real-world data suggest up to roughly 65 percent quit within a year, and a 2026 meta-regression finds about 60 percent of lost weight returns within a year of stopping (individual studies vary). The discontinuation moment is unowned: prescribers lose the patient, gyms never see them, and regain triggers shame and churn.
ideas.solution: A program keyed to the last-dose date: taper coordination with the prescriber, protein and resistance-training progression, weekly connected-scale weigh-ins, human coach check-ins on hunger and food noise, and pre-agreed re-start triggers (for example +3 percent regain) that route the patient back to the prescriber. Delivered by app plus partner gyms.
ideas.why_now: Oral GLP-1s at $149-299 cash (Wegovy pill launched Dec 2025/Jan 2026, orforglipron in April 2026) make starting cheap and stopping easy; about 1 in 8 US adults report currently taking one; cash-pay churn is the biggest leak in prescriber P&Ls.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-300 per enrollee paid by the prescriber as a retention and win-back tool (or $199 patient-paid), plus a revenue share on patients who restart therapy.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the prescriber, not the patient: the off-ramp is a retention product for the clinic's P&L, and a regain alert doubles as a win-back lead. Evidence on who regains is mixed, so a regain-risk model built from your own cohort becomes the proprietary asset.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 3-5 independent clinics or med spas, enroll 30 patients ending therapy using an off-the-shelf connected scale, messaging tool and a lifting template, and track 90-day weight, lean-mass proxy and restart rate versus each clinic's history to use as the sales proof.

ideas.title: Turnkey Recovery Amenity Operator for Landlords
ideas.one_liner: Operate managed sauna-and-cold-plunge suites inside apartment and mixed-use buildings, paid a flat monthly fee by the landlord.
ideas.customer: Owners and operators of multifamily, mixed-use and office buildings with underused fitness rooms and an amenity-arms-race problem.
ideas.problem: Insiders treat recovery as a consumer studio business (one brand went from zero to 25 contrast-therapy studios in about 20 months and plans 100 more), with retail rent, foot-traffic marketing and wet/hot-room liability. Meanwhile landlords already own the square footage and want differentiators, but cannot operate saunas and plunge tubs (cleaning, water treatment, safety, insurance).
ideas.solution: Design, install (modular saunas and tubs) and operate a recovery suite: booking app, resident access control, daily cleaning and water testing, camera-free safety monitoring, waiver and insurance management. The landlord pays a flat monthly operating fee; residents can pay small fees for guests or premium hours.
ideas.why_now: Nordic-style social wellness attendance grew about 33 percent in 2025, sauna and cold-plunge hardware is a $1B+ market and getting cheaper, and HSA-linked home sauna sales show pre-tax demand exists even without a studio.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-8k per month per property operating fee (or revenue share above a threshold) plus $40-120k build-out margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The best customer for the sauna boom is not the Gen Z consumer but the landlord: acquisition cost is one sales call instead of a marketing budget, and what the landlord is really buying is zero-liability operation, not wellness.
ideas.first_30_days: Cold-outreach 100 mid-size multifamily owners in one metro with underused amenity rooms, then pilot one building with a rented modular sauna and a $3k plunge tub on a 90-day contract at about $2.5k per month while tracking resident usage and renewal intent.

ideas.title: Referee Body-Cams and Abuse Evidence Layer
ideas.one_liner: A clip-on camera and incident-report service that gives youth and high school officials proof and gives leagues grounds to ban abusive spectators.
ideas.customer: State high school associations, officials' associations, youth leagues and tournament operators, paying per official per season.
ideas.problem: About 50,000 high school officials have left since 2018, more than 70 percent of new referees quit within three years, and half report feeling unsafe. Insiders assume pay raises fix the shortage, but abuse is the driver and leagues cannot sanction parents or coaches without evidence, so games run short-staffed or get cancelled.
ideas.solution: A $50-100 chest-mounted camera or phone clip with audio; speech-to-text flags threats and slurs; league admins get a one-click incident packet (timestamps, transcript, clip) tied to a spectator code of conduct; officials get a private 'safe report' button. Leagues use the evidence to issue bans and support refs.
ideas.why_now: 2026 shortage coverage (New York, Utah and others) consistently blames abuse; cheap on-device transcription and body cams make this a $60 problem; national bodies such as USA Volleyball have created formal harassment-response programs, showing appetite.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-90 per official per season (hardware included) plus $500-3k per year per league for the admin dashboard; potential insurer partnerships.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a safety problem, not a pay problem, and the true buyer is the league's risk manager. Recording laws vary by state, so the product is policy-first (posted notices, opt-in associations) and starts where the association mandates it.
ideas.first_30_days: Pilot with one regional officials association (about 100 officials) using off-the-shelf action cams and a transcription pipeline, draft a spectator-policy template with a local attorney, run one season of evidence, and convert two leagues into paying customers.

ideas.title: Bone-First Strength Program for Women 45+
ideas.one_liner: A gym-delivered lifting and impact program for perimenopausal women, sold on DEXA-verified bone and muscle results.
ideas.customer: Women aged roughly 42-60 paying $79-149 per month, delivered through independent gyms, Pilates and strength studios and PT clinics that license the program.
ideas.problem: Women's fitness tech is fixated on cycle-syncing even though current evidence for cycle effects on performance is inconclusive, while midlife women (an 'invisible cohort' in sports science) face accelerating bone and muscle loss, worsened for those on GLP-1 drugs. Gyms sell toning and never measure the outcome that matters.
ideas.solution: A 24-week program of progressive heavy lifting, impact and balance work, with DEXA at baseline, 6 and 12 months via partner scan providers, simple bone-loading dose tracking with a hip or wrist sensor, coach training and a results dashboard studios use for retention. Positioned as wellness and performance with a physician advisor, not treatment.
ideas.why_now: Retail DEXA scans have dropped to roughly sub-$100, menopause is a mainstream topic, wearable makers are pouring money into women's health, perimenopause research is accelerating in 2026, and GLP-1 adoption has made bone and lean-mass loss a mass-market worry.
ideas.revenue_model: Member fees $79-149 per month; studio license $299-499 per month plus $30 per member; scan affiliate margin of $10-20 per scan.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The moat is the outcome measurement: 'X percent of members held or gained bone density at 12 months' is a claim no gym can currently make, and the resulting dataset is valuable to clinicians and researchers. Cycle-syncing is a distraction from the larger midlife need.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 25 women aged 45-60 through two local strength gyms, book baseline DEXA scans with a retail or mobile provider, run a 12-week pilot with a physician advisor, and sign three studios to license the program off the interim results.

ideas.title: Transfer-Portal Durability Passport for College Athletes
ideas.one_liner: An athlete-owned, verified injury and load history that programs will demand before they commit six figures of revenue share.
ideas.customer: College programs (general managers, sports medicine, compliance), collectives and agents pay for verified dossiers; athletes get their file free and own it.
ideas.problem: Chain: the House settlement lets schools pay athletes up to about $20.5M in 2025-26, unlimited transfers and the June 2026 shift to a five-year eligibility clock make multi-year, money-bearing roster bets, yet there is no standard electronic medical record across schools. Injury history moves by phone call and rumor: athletes fear disclosure, programs fear buying a torn ACL, and agents cannot prove durability.
ideas.solution: A consent-based portal where athletes' athletic trainers upload structured injury and return-to-play summaries, a standardized functional battery (jump/landing, isometric strength, hop tests) run at partner performance gyms, and optional load history exports from Catapult or WHOOP. The athlete chooses who sees what; the receiving program pays for a standardized, verified dossier.
ideas.why_now: Revenue-share contracts, unlimited transfers and the 2026 eligibility overhaul raise the financial stakes of injuries; the proposed Protect College Sports Act would add post-eligibility medical coverage duties and privacy protections; state privacy laws and HIPRA push consent-based data handling.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-300 per verified passport paid by the receiving program; $10-25k per year per program for scouting and post-signing baselines; $99 per athlete from agents.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The athlete, not the school, must own the file: that is what makes disclosure acceptable and gives buyers something they can trust. It is a Carfax for players, and the customers now have real money at risk.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 mid-major and D2 basketball and volleyball athletes entering the portal through 3-4 friendly agents, build the consent form and one-page dossier, run 10 test sessions at a local performance gym, and pitch three assistant coaches or GMs on paying $200 per dossier.

ideas.title: Thermal Safety Certification for Recovery Studios
ideas.one_liner: Staff certification, medication-aware intake screening and water-quality logging that insurers will soon require of sauna and cold-plunge operators.
ideas.customer: Contrast-therapy studios, gym recovery rooms, hotels and spas, paying monthly per location.
ideas.problem: Chain: studios are rolling out at speed (one brand added 25 locations in about 20 months and plans 100 more), so hundreds of new hires with no clinical training run 190F rooms and shared 40F tubs; customers increasingly take GLP-1s, blood-pressure meds or diuretics that raise fainting and dehydration risk; shared plunge water has no consistent standard and health departments are unsure how to classify it. One serious incident will trigger insurer exclusions and regulator attention.
ideas.solution: Three-part kit: a 90-minute 'Thermal Host' certification with annual refresh; tablet check-in screening (conditions and medications mapped to green/yellow/red session guidance plus waiver logging); and a water sensor pack (ORP, pH, chlorine, temperature) that auto-generates logs for inspectors and insurers.
ideas.why_now: The recovery boom (Nordic-style attendance up about 33 percent in 2025), mass GLP-1 use (about 1 in 8 adults), and no existing standard mean insurers and health departments are about to look for controls.
ideas.revenue_model: $99-199 per month per location, $39 per staff certification, sensor rental $49 per month per tub, plus insurer or broker referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Be the standard before the incident: insurers would rather subsidize a certification than write exclusions, and the screening data is a wedge to premium programs. GLP-1 plus heat is the specific collision no one is training for.
ideas.first_30_days: Draft the protocol with a sports-medicine physician and a pool-operations consultant, sell it to 5 independent studios in one metro at a discounted founding rate, and ask two studio-focused insurance brokers for a premium credit for certified locations.

ideas.title: Proof-of-Workout Fraud Shield for Fitness Incentives
ideas.one_liner: A verification API that scores whether a gym visit or workout really happened, priced per verified event.
ideas.customer: Administrators of pay-per-visit fitness benefits (regional Medicare Advantage plans, employer stipend platforms), movement-reward and fitness-betting apps.
ideas.problem: Chain: Medicare Advantage plans are trimming fitness benefits (93 percent offered one in 2026 versus 95 percent in 2025, more cuts expected) and payers and employers shift toward pay-per-verified-visit and reward models (one employer wellness network lists over 20,000 employer partners), so money follows check-ins and step counts. Fraud (shared QR codes, spoofed steps, ghost visits, inflated gym counts) becomes the margin killer and nobody sells fraud scoring built for fitness.
ideas.solution: An SDK and API combining phone attestation, gym BLE or Wi-Fi beacons, wearable heart-rate and motion consistency, GPS and barometer, and device-sharing graphs into an authenticity score with an audit trail, ring detection and a dispute workflow for gyms.
ideas.why_now: Benefit cuts push payers to pay-per-use, wearable aggregator APIs make cross-signal checks cheap, and mobile attestation is mature; HIPRA-style consent rules make audit trails a requirement.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.05-0.20 per verified event with a $2-5k monthly minimum, plus a gain share on recovered fraud.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a labeled fraud dataset: once you process millions of visits you can sell audits to payers, and because you are neutral infrastructure you compete with no wearable or gym software vendor.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 2-3 reward or betting apps or one regional benefit administrator, run their last 90 days of check-ins through a prototype scorer, quantify suspected fraud, and charge $5-10k for the audit before integrating.

ideas.title: Preseason ACL Screening for Girls' Clubs
ideas.one_liner: A 10-second phone-video landing screen at tryouts that flags risky mechanics and routes athletes to prevention programs and PT.
ideas.customer: Youth club directors and high school athletic directors (pay $8-15 per athlete); PT and sports-medicine clinics (pay for referred athletes and return-to-sport testing).
ideas.problem: Chain: women's pro leagues drive rapid growth of girls' club sports, more year-round load raises ACL tears (girls' rates are several times boys'), and PT and orthopedic capacity is short (outpatient PT vacancy rates around 17 percent, Medicare pressure pushing clinics to cash-pay), while return-to-sport decisions still rely on subjective checks. Nobody screens 400,000 girls before the season.
ideas.solution: Phone or existing AI-camera footage of a drop jump and single-leg landing, analyzed by markerless pose estimation; flagged athletes get a tailored FIFA-11+-style program by SMS video and a 4-week re-test; PT partners pay for return-to-sport test packages using the same tech. Framed as movement-quality coaching with measurable pre/post improvement, not injury prediction.
ideas.why_now: Open-source markerless biomechanics is now good enough for field use, AI cameras are already in clubs (roughly $949 plus subscription), and cash-pay PT clinics need a top-of-funnel; parents already spend thousands per year on club sports.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-15 per athlete billed to the club or added at registration; $1.5-3k per year per PT clinic partner; $49 per return-to-sport test.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the club (liability and differentiation), and the PT clinic pays for demand. Screens are weak predictors, so a small validation study and honest positioning as an intervention-adherence tool is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with two clubs at tryouts (about 200 athletes), a sports PT clinic and a university biomechanist to validate against reference measures, produce a one-page athlete report, and take a $500 sponsorship from the clinic.

ideas.title: Hybrid-Race-in-a-Box Rentals for Gyms
ideas.one_liner: Rentable station kits, timing, waivers, insurance and sanitation protocols so any gym can run a Hyrox-style event for members.
ideas.customer: Independent gyms and CrossFit-style boxes (pay $2.5-4k per event); secondary: run-club organizers and corporate wellness days.
ideas.problem: Chain: Hyrox's global boom (events selling out, new markets such as Kuala Lumpur in December 2026) makes members demand local competitions, but official events are capacity-limited and licensed; local copycats need eight stations of gear, timing, heat management and a medical plan; and the Beijing incident (an athlete kept racing after soiling herself on shared equipment, prompting an apology and new biohazard rules) shows sanitation is a brand-level risk. Nobody sells a standardized, insured kit.
ideas.solution: A trailerized 8-station kit with standard loading specs, chip or QR bib timing through a phone app, wipe-down protocol cards and biohazard kit, medical response plan, waiver and event-insurance pack, and a results page. The gym sells tickets; we take rental plus a per-athlete fee.
ideas.why_now: Hybrid racing went mainstream in 2025-26, hygiene and safety incidents have made organizers seek documented protocols, and used sleds and ergs are cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $2.5-4k per event rental plus about $5 per athlete for timing and insurance; sell kits to multi-gym operators at $18-30k.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not the format but the logistics and liability packaging for local operators; for a gym the payoff is member retention and lead generation from ticket buyers who are not yet members.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy $12-15k of used sleds, ballast and ergs, run a first event with a partner gym to document cost per athlete, offer three other gyms discounted rentals, and build a small QR-bib timing page.

ideas.title: Cancellation Compliance for Regional Gym Chains
ideas.one_liner: A drop-in cancel-and-freeze portal that meets each state's auto-renewal rules and writes straight into the billing system.
ideas.customer: Regional gym and studio chains with 10-300 locations still using in-person or certified-mail cancellations, and franchisors.
ideas.problem: The FTC's national click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, but enforcement continues (the FTC sued Fitness International/LA Fitness over cancellation hurdles), state auto-renewal laws demand online cancellation if you joined online, and New York City's own click-to-cancel rule takes effect October 1, 2026. Chains run legacy contracts and billing where cancellation is manual, so exposure is AG settlements and class actions.
ideas.solution: A white-labeled 'Cancel, Pause, Downgrade' portal with a jurisdiction rules engine (notice periods, save-offer limits, refund proration, confirmations) that writes to the chain's billing platform through API or RPA, with audit logs and legally bounded retention offers.
ideas.why_now: NYC's October 1, 2026 deadline, the FTC's restart of subscription rulemaking, and active state AG scrutiny create a dated trigger with budget.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per location per month plus $2k setup; share of saved revenue on approved retention flows.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Compliance opens the door, retention pays for it: a compliant flow with legally allowed save offers often lifts net retention versus the friction chains use today, so the CFO buys it. The moat is the multi-state rules matrix plus billing-system integrations.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a rules matrix for 10 states plus NYC with a consumer-protection lawyer, sell a $1k mystery-shop 'compliance scan' of each chain's cancellation flow to 20 regional chains, and convert two into design partners.

ideas.title: Mindbody Escape Hatch: Studio Migration Concierge
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee service that moves a studio's members, class packs and payment tokens off Mindbody without losing revenue.
ideas.customer: Boutique studios, gyms, yoga and Pilates operators on Mindbody (about 40,000 businesses) paying $159-699 per month plus marketplace commissions.
ideas.problem: After the ClassPass/Mindbody/EGYM combination (a $7.5B deal completed in 2026), owners report about 23.5 percent effective marketplace commissions and a roughly $500 data-export fee on cancellation. Lock-in is not the software but the card-on-file payment tokens and member history, so owners fear migration will churn members.
ideas.solution: A fixed-fee migration ($1.5-3k): export clients, attendance, waivers, packs and memberships; execute PCI-compliant processor-to-processor token migration; map intro offers and unlimited plans; rebuild schedule widgets; run parallel billing checks; and message members by SMS. Target alternative platforms pay a bounty per migrated studio.
ideas.why_now: Consolidation gave studios a reason to re-evaluate, ClassPass is rolling out studio-friendly policies in response to complaints, and processors now support token migration.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-3k per migration plus $200-400 bounty per studio from the receiving software vendor and an optional $99 per month retention audit.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The moat is edge-case knowledge (paused members, unlimited plans, refunds, tokens), not software, and rival vendors will pay you for customers because their own acquisition cost is high.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer five free migration audits in studio-owner communities, pick two target platforms, run three at-cost pilot migrations, and turn the playbook into a checklist and pricing page.

ideas.title: Remote Athletic Trainer Coverage for Rural Schools
ideas.one_liner: A subscription sideline triage line, protocol library and documentation service that stretches one licensed athletic trainer across many schools.
ideas.customer: Rural and small school districts, state athletic associations and school risk pools paying $6-20k per school per season.
ideas.problem: NATA-cited figures show about 41 percent of Kansas schools and 68 percent of Oklahoma schools lack an athletic trainer, only about a third of Arkansas schools have one, and Massachusetts does not require one (Boston Globe, September 28, 2026). Coaches make return-to-play calls and handle concussions, heat and cardiac emergencies ad hoc, and districts carry the liability.
ideas.solution: Licensed ATs run a game-time line where coaches call or video-chat for triage; ATs guide return-to-play, do next-day follow-ups, document per state concussion law, and supply emergency action plans and coach training. Optional phase two: AT review of clips from schools' existing AI cameras.
ideas.why_now: 2026 shortage coverage keeps escalating, legislatures are debating mandates, and schools already own cheap AI cameras and video-call tools.
ideas.revenue_model: $6-20k per school per season, district-wide contracts, risk-pool discounts, and per-event tournament coverage fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Training more ATs will not fix this within five years; extending each AT's reach 5-10x will. School insurers and risk pools care about concussion litigation and will subsidize it, so it is sold as liability reduction rather than healthcare.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired ATs licensed in one state, pitch 10 districts on a 4-week football-season pilot at $2.5k, and pitch that state's school risk pool on co-funding.

ideas.title: Risk and Insurance Stack for Pickleball Venues
ideas.one_liner: Incident logging, e-waivers, court-safety audits and an insurance program that make independent racquet venues insurable at fair prices.
ideas.customer: Independent indoor and outdoor pickleball and padel venue operators, plus HOAs and municipal recreation departments.
ideas.problem: Indoor pickleball operators report difficulty finding coverage, typical policies carry $1-5M general liability, injuries rose about 6.8x between 2017 and 2022, and noise disputes now end in lawsuits. Insurers lack venue-level data, so they price the category rather than the operator.
ideas.solution: Step one: $149-299 per month software with e-waivers, incident reporting, a photo-evidence court, lighting and fencing audit checklist and staff training. Step two: use the aggregated data to place operators with specialty carriers as a broker or MGA and negotiate premium credits for documented venues.
ideas.why_now: Venue counts have boomed while commentators now say the boom is starting to crack, which makes insurers and lenders demand evidence; no standard exists.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS $149-299 per venue per month plus 10-15 percent broker or MGA commission on premiums of $8-30k per policy.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Data is the product: when insurers lack venue-level evidence they price to the average, so the operator who documents beats the average. Start as software, then capture the insurance economics.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a licensed broker, audit 10 venues in one metro, produce an insurer-ready risk dossier for each, and take 20 dossiers to two specialty carriers.

ideas.title: PFAS Turf Audits and Replacement Planning
ideas.one_liner: Field-by-field PFAS and regulatory risk audits plus replacement bid packages for school districts and parks departments with aging synthetic turf.
ideas.customer: School district facilities directors, athletic directors, municipal parks and recreation departments and colleges.
ideas.problem: Thousands of synthetic fields installed in the 2010s are reaching end of life just as PFAS rules bite: New York's ban on selling PFAS-containing turf takes effect December 31, 2026, California's restriction on PFAS in covered surfaces began January 1, 2026, and other states (New Jersey, Maine) have bills to pause purchases. Districts do not know what is under their fields, may not be able to buy what they always bought, and face bond votes and parent pressure.
ideas.solution: A $2.5-8k audit per district: field inventory (age, product, manufacturer), lab testing of fibers and infill through an accredited partner, legal exposure summary, lifecycle-cost comparison of synthetic, PFAS-free, hybrid and natural grass, and turnkey bid documents; then project-management and referral fees.
ideas.why_now: 2026 effective dates, active parent and environmental groups, and pending state bills create urgent, budgeted decisions.
ideas.revenue_model: $2.5-8k audits, testing pass-through margin, 2-4 percent project-management fees on $500k-1.5M projects, supplier referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody owns 'what is my turf made of' data and manufacturers will not volunteer it. Sitting between district, lab and contractor makes you the neutral spec writer who controls the RFP.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a public-records inventory of turf fields in New York from bond documents and board minutes, pitch 50 districts, line up an accredited lab, and sell three audits.

ideas.title: Muscle Ultrasound Scans as a Gym Vital Sign
ideas.one_liner: A five-minute, AI-read thigh ultrasound that tells GLP-1 users and lifters whether they are keeping their muscle.
ideas.customer: Gyms, GLP-1 and weight-loss clinics and PT clinics; consumers pay $29-49 per scan, clinics pay per-scan licenses.
ideas.problem: Studies suggest 20-50 percent of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can be lean mass, but scales, bioimpedance and photos cannot show muscle and DEXA is costly and inconvenient. Trainers and clinics have no cheap, objective muscle metric to motivate clients or steer dosing and training.
ideas.solution: A coach scans the quadriceps with a handheld probe; AI segments rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness and echogenicity; results are trended over time and against a cohort. Positioned as general wellness muscle-thickness tracking that integrates with training and nutrition plans, not diagnosis.
ideas.why_now: Handheld ultrasound now shows excellent agreement with cart systems for quadriceps thickness (ICC above 0.9 in a 2025 study), automated AI muscle segmentation is maturing, muscle loss on GLP-1s was a headline debate at ADA 2026, and the FDA's wellness posture is looser.
ideas.revenue_model: $29-49 per scan retail; gym device-plus-software rental at $299-499 per month; per-scan fees for clinics.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Trend in thickness, not absolute mass, is precise enough to change behavior. It is a retention and upsell tool for gyms (more strength coaching for people who can see the muscle they are protecting).
ideas.first_30_days: Buy two handheld probes, validate against DEXA on 50 volunteers with a partner clinic, run scan days at three gyms and one GLP-1 clinic at $39 per scan, and sign the first monthly device subscription.

ideas.title: Swimmer-Distress Drones for Endurance Events
ideas.one_liner: A race-day service using thermal-camera drones and AI to spot swimmers in trouble before rescue boats do.
ideas.customer: Triathlon, open-water swim and Ironman-style race directors, event insurers, and municipalities running beach swims.
ideas.problem: Most triathlon deaths occur in the swim, and safety still depends on kayaks and volunteers scanning choppy water. A study at the 2018 IRONMAN Mont-Tremblant found drones identified 1 of 5 distress events before rescue boats saw them, and human spotters tire.
ideas.solution: An operator-plus-software service: one or two drones with visible and thermal cameras track the swim course, AI flags prolonged stillness, vertical posture or flailing, and alerts go to the rescue coordinator by radio app, with a post-race report for insurers. Later add wearable tags and AED delivery.
ideas.why_now: Thermal drone cameras and edge vision models are cheap, FAA rules for wider drone operations are advancing, and open-water race participation is climbing.
ideas.revenue_model: $2.5-8k per event, annual series contracts, and insurer-funded discounts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The pain sits with event insurers and small race directors, for whom one fatality can end the event, so the pitch is loss reduction with data. AI is valuable mainly because it does not get tired.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy two drones (about $8k), recruit a licensed Part 107 pilot and a lifeguard consultant, provide free coverage at two local swims to collect labeled footage, and pitch 10 small triathlon directors a $1.5k pilot.

ideas.title: Exoskeleton Hike Rentals for Active Older Adults
ideas.one_liner: Trailhead rental hubs and guided exo-hikes that let 60-80 year-olds keep climbing with powered hip assist.
ideas.customer: Active adults 55+ (pay $70-120 per day), outdoor retailers and outfitters, senior-living activity directors and trail-gateway towns.
ideas.problem: Consumer exoskeletons now exist ($900-2,300, with the leader's models at about $2,000-2,300) but buyers hesitate to spend that on something they have never tried, and older hikers quietly stop hiking as knees and hips fade.
ideas.solution: A rental fleet with fitting, safety briefing and waivers, guided group hikes, retailer rental corners, and monthly exo-walks for senior living communities. Renters get a credit toward purchase and we earn affiliate commissions.
ideas.why_now: Consumer hip-assist exoskeletons reached the $900-2,300 range with heavy marketing, the leading brand is pushing an 'offline' era with retail and rental hubs, and the active-older-adult demographic is driving the category.
ideas.revenue_model: $79 per day rentals, $30 per person guided add-ons, 8-12 percent affiliate on purchases, retail rental-program fees and $1-2k per month senior-living contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is trial, not price, and manufacturers lack local operators; a small team can own the try-before-you-buy channel. The real work is waivers, fitting and injury protocols, which are also the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy or borrow four units (about $8k), set up demo weekends at one or two outdoor shops or campgrounds near a popular trail, run a senior-center exo-walk, and start charging rentals from week two.

ideas.title: Compute-Heated Pools and Saunas
ideas.one_liner: Install small immersion-cooled compute clusters in municipal pools, Ys and recovery studios so the servers pay for the heat.
ideas.customer: Municipal pools, YMCAs and hotels with heavy heating bills, recovery studios with saunas, and the AI batch-inference buyers who rent the compute.
ideas.problem: Pools and sauna rooms are among the largest energy line items in public and wellness facilities and many public pools are cut when budgets tighten, while AI compute needs cooling and dumps its waste heat.
ideas.solution: Deploy a 20-50 kW 'digital boiler' in the plant room that heats pool or sauna water through a heat exchanger, sell the compute to latency-tolerant inference or batch customers, and give the facility free or discounted heat. First product: a single-site pilot funded by a state energy grant and reserved compute.
ideas.why_now: A UK pilot at Exmouth Leisure Centre (a 28 kW cluster) reportedly cut the pool's gas use by 62 percent and saved about 24,000 dollars a year while the operator paid for the electricity; AI compute scarcity and edge inference demand are high in 2026 and decarbonization grants are available.
ideas.revenue_model: Compute revenue shared with the host, monthly heat fee or discount, and grants; gross margin from selling the heat.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Both sides get paid: the compute buyer gets free cooling and the pool gets free heat, and a pool is a 24/7 constant heat sink unlike offices. The real customer is the compute buyer, with pools as cheap distributed real estate. Capital needs are real, so lead with a grant-funded pilot.
ideas.first_30_days: Find a gas-heated pool operator and a champion on the board, sign an MOU, commission a 10-20 kW pilot design with an immersion-cooling vendor, apply to two energy grant programs, and pre-sell reserved compute to two batch-inference customers.

ideas.title: Ceiling-Camera Auto-Logging for Strength Gyms
ideas.one_liner: Cameras that watch the lifting floor and automatically log every athlete's sets, reps, load and bar speed with no phone.
ideas.customer: Independent strength gyms, CrossFit boxes, powerlifting clubs and high school and college weight rooms paying $199-499 per month.
ideas.problem: Progress tracking is the strongest retention lever in lifting, but manual logging is tedious so most members skip it, and coaches at high athlete ratios cannot see everyone's sets or spot stalls.
ideas.solution: Two to four ceiling cameras plus an edge box; vision models recognize the exercise, plate colors (load), rep count and bar velocity; lifters are identified by wristband or QR rather than faces; a coach dashboard flags stalls, form drift and missed sessions and a member app fills logs automatically.
ideas.why_now: 2025-26 vision foundation models handle exercise and object recognition at the edge on cheap hardware, and tightening biometric privacy laws push products toward non-facial identification.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-499 per gym per month plus $1.5-3k install; school weight-room licenses; velocity-based-training analytics as an add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the coach or owner, not the member: automatic logging gives coaches visibility that drives retention and coaching upsells, a Hudl for the weight room. Avoiding face recognition sidesteps biometric-law exposure.
ideas.first_30_days: Install DIY hardware (about $800) in two friendly gyms, label two weeks of squat, bench and deadlift footage with plate detection, offer a free three-month pilot, and measure log completion and member retention to justify $299 per month.

ideas.title: Orphan Appliance Parts, Crowdsourced From Repair Techs
