ideas.one_liner: Quirky (dead 2015) crowdsourced gadgets from hobbyist inventors; the 2026 version prints the discontinued $6 plastic part that keeps a $900 appliance out of the landfill, and pays the repair tech who specced it a royalty.
ideas.customer: Independent appliance repair shops (about 10-20 techs per metro market) and multifamily property-maintenance teams that manage hundreds of identical fridges, washers and dishwashers; DIY owners and EU repair cafes come second via marketplace listings.
ideas.problem: A brittle plastic piece (fridge door bin, dishwasher rack wheel, washer lid-lock striker, range knob, vacuum gear) is discontinued, backordered for weeks, or OEM-priced at $50-90. Techs condemn a machine over a $6 part, and landlords swap whole units. Techs see the same failure dozens of times but have no channel to monetize that knowledge.
ideas.solution: A tech texts a photo and model number. An AI-assisted CAD step plus human check produces a measured model. The part is printed in nylon or carbon-filled PETG through Xometry/Craftcloud-type bureaus, or a small in-house farm. It gets a SKU page, a fit guarantee (free reprint if wrong) and a 10% lifetime royalty to the originating tech. Non-safety-critical parts only: no heating elements, gas, or oven door latches. Shops pay $29/mo for a private request queue, 48-hour dispatch and a discount. Property managers get bulk catalogs per building.
ideas.why_now: The EU Right to Repair Directive's national transposition deadline passed on 31 July 2026. It requires spare parts at reasonable prices and bars manufacturers from blocking independent repairers who use compatible or 3D-printed parts. Several US states (CA, NY, MN, OR) have repair laws. Photo-to-CAD tools are good enough and print-on-demand bureaus are cheap. Tariffs have pushed new-appliance prices up, so repair economics are better than in 2015.
ideas.revenue_model: Part sales at $18-35 (roughly 50-65% gross margin after print and shipping); $29/mo shop membership; annual bulk contracts with property managers; royalty payouts as the growth loop. Later, license CAD to mid-size OEMs that need cheap R2R-compliant spares for out-of-production models.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Quirky's crowd was the wrong crowd: hobbyist inventors with no ground truth about what breaks. The right crowd already exists in the field: techs who see failure modes daily and lack a way to get paid for that. The right buyer is not the DIYer but a pro or landlord for whom a $12 part avoids a $900 replacement. The orphan-part long tail is what 3D printing is naturally good at, and the R2R text neutralizes OEM opposition.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick fridges and dishwashers from 2005-2015. Mine r/appliancerepair, eBay sold listings and out-of-stock parts pages for the 25 most-failed brittle plastics. Model and print them via two bureaus and list on eBay, Etsy and Shopify with the fit guarantee. Recruit 15 local techs from Facebook groups with the royalty offer, and pilot with 3 property managers. Under $10k of spend; target 150 orders.

ideas.title: Josephine Reborn: Permit Concierge for Home Kitchens
ideas.one_liner: Josephine's home-cooked-meal marketplace was boxed in by health law; California's MEHKO law now licenses home restaurants, so build the permit concierge and a compliant direct-to-consumer storefront, not another marketplace.
ideas.customer: Home cooks, especially immigrant and regional-cuisine specialists (tamales, Armenian, Korean, Oaxacan, Filipino), in Los Angeles County and the roughly 19 California jurisdictions that had authorized MEHKOs as of May 2026. Many already sell via Instagram and WhatsApp without a permit.
ideas.problem: MEHKO caps are 30 meals/day, 90/week and roughly $107k/year. Applying costs about $597 plus about $347/yr in LA County, plus food-handler certification, menu SOPs, labels, sales logs and inspections. Third-party delivery apps are restricted, so cooks cannot just list on DoorDash. No tool enforces the caps, produces inspector-ready records, or helps neighbors find them, and paperwork is mostly in English.
ideas.solution: A permit concierge ($249-399 one-time) that completes the application, SOPs and multilingual allergen labels. Then a $20/mo cook operating system: link-in-bio storefront with pre-orders and pickup windows, automatic sell-out at 30/day and 90/week, temperature and sales logs exported in the county's format, and Stripe payments. Demand comes from neighborhood 'Friday drop' maps and newsletters and workplace pickup clusters. Cooks own their customers; there is no marketplace.
ideas.why_now: MEHKO adoption is spreading county by county (17 counties plus Berkeley and Long Beach by May 2026), with LA County running an active program. Restaurant prices are high, social commerce is normal, and AI makes multilingual SOPs and labels nearly free. A few early MEHKO startups exist, so the opening is to be permit-first, multilingual and neighborhood-by-neighborhood.
ideas.revenue_model: $249-399 permit concierge fee; $20/mo per cook SaaS; roughly 1% payments margin; affiliate income from food-handler training and liability insurance. Later, a bulk-permitting contract with counties that want cleaner inspection records.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The marketplace was the illegal or unscalable part, and under MEHKO it is structurally limited to direct-to-consumer sales. The scarce asset is the permit, and the winning product is compliance and storefront tooling that turns each cook into her own licensed restaurant. Enforcing the meal caps in software becomes a feature, and it makes the vendor the county health department's preferred partner.
ideas.first_30_days: Attend LA County MEHKO office hours. Find 10 cooks on Instagram (#lahomecook, #tamales) and do their applications free in exchange for case studies. Build the storefront with Shopify or Stripe plus a no-code cap rule. Target 5 issued permits within about 60 days, then start charging the $20/mo.

ideas.title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
ideas.one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
ideas.customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
ideas.problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
ideas.solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
ideas.why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
ideas.revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
ideas.first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

ideas.title: Quibi for Home-Care Aides: Serialized Compliance Training
ideas.one_liner: Quibi's 90-second premium episodes failed as a consumer subscription; as a serialized vertical drama that home-care aides watch to fulfill their mandatory annual training hours, the same format has a captive, budgeted buyer.
ideas.customer: Owners and training directors of home-health and home-care agencies with 20-500 aides. Medicare-certified home health agencies must give each aide annual in-service training (12 hours under federal rules), and many states add annual hours for personal-care aides.
ideas.problem: Caregiver turnover benchmarks around 75% in 2025. Required training is slide decks and quizzes that workers click through on phones, yet client falls, infections, abuse-reporting failures and survey citations trace back to it. Agencies pay for training that neither sticks nor improves retention.
ideas.solution: A private serialized story of two aides and a difficult client. Each 90-second vertical episode ends on a decision (dementia sundowning, family conflict, suspected neglect); the answer unlocks the next episode. Delivered by SMS or WhatsApp link with no app, in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Haitian Creole. An RN advisor approves content, quiz logs map to training-hour documentation, and supervisors get a completion dashboard. AI-assisted production plus human voice actors keeps a season at low tens of thousands of dollars.
ideas.why_now: Microdrama apps are booming: industry trackers put short-drama in-app revenue near $3B in 2025 and forecasts of roughly $8B in 2026, so the habit and format exist. Reported AI-assisted production budgets of $15-80k per series are far below traditional costs. Home-care demand is surging while the workforce shrinks.
ideas.revenue_model: $6-10 per aide per month with a $300/mo agency minimum, annual contracts; bespoke episodes on an agency's own policies at $3-5k each; same engine later sold to nursing homes, restaurants and hotels.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Quibi's format was fine and its buyer was wrong. Consumers would not pay $8/mo for premium clips, but mandatory compliance budgets are captive and the outcomes (completion, quiz retention, incident reports, quits) are measurable. Frontline workers already binge microdramas on the same phones, so the drama does the engagement work and the compliance layer does the billing.
ideas.first_30_days: Write 6 episodes on three topics (dementia behaviors, fall prevention, abuse reporting) with an RN advisor and produce them for under $5k. Pitch 30 agencies through state home-care association lists and LinkedIn. Run free 30-day pilots at 3 agencies, comparing completion and quiz scores against their current slides, then convert to $500/mo contracts.

ideas.title: Bot-Proof Local Comments: Verified Neighbors, Pseudonymous
ideas.one_liner: Secret and Yik Yak died of unaccountable anonymity and Digg's March 2026 relaunch died of bots; the missing primitive is 'one real human, from this place, no real name', and local newsrooms and city councils will pay for it.
ideas.customer: Independent and nonprofit local newsrooms (hundreds exist) that have switched off comments, and city, county and school-board clerks running public comment for hearings on rezonings, data centers and levies.
ideas.problem: Newsrooms disabled comment sections because of toxicity and bots, so local conversation moved to Facebook groups. Public bodies get astroturf and AI-generated comment floods (the 2017 FCC net-neutrality docket was later found mostly fake by New York's attorney general) and cannot tell residents from out-of-area campaigns or bots.
ideas.solution: An embeddable comment and public-comment widget. Each person verifies once via a state mobile ID in Apple or Google Wallet with address check, or a postcard PIN or voter-file match as fallback, then posts under a pseudonym. The platform attests only 'verified human, resident of ZIP or ward X'. Public bodies get a verified-resident tally (for example, '412 verified residents commented, 78% opposed, 61 from Ward 3'). One credential works across the paper, council and school board, and publishers never see identity.
ideas.why_now: Digg's open beta launched 14 January 2026 and shut on 14 March 2026 after bot and AI-agent floods. Agents can now write plausible public comments at scale. Mobile IDs in phone wallets make cheap, high-assurance verification possible. Local news funders are paying for audience-trust infrastructure.
ideas.revenue_model: $200-1,500/mo per newsroom; $500-3,000/mo per municipality or agency for a verified public-comment portal; per-verification fees ($0.50-1.50) sponsored by foundations or civic funders; later, verified local polling panels.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Anonymity was never the fatal flaw; unverifiable anonymity was. In a bot-saturated internet, 'provably a real neighbor' becomes the scarce good, and local institutions already need it but cannot buy it. The credential also compounds: a resident verified once for the newspaper is reusable for council, school board and library levy comments.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 small newsrooms through nonprofit-news networks to run a verified-comment pilot on one hot local issue (rezoning or data center) using SMS or postcard plus voter-file match. Publish the verified-tally story, then pitch the same town's clerk a public-comment pilot. Charge $250/mo after the pilot.

ideas.title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
ideas.one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
ideas.customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
ideas.problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
ideas.solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
ideas.why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
ideas.revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.

ideas.title: Immigration Deadline Sentinel for Work-Permit Households
ideas.one_liner: The wealthy keep immigration counsel on retainer to calendar, file early and bridge gaps; for $20/mo, give H-4, OPT, asylum-applicant and DACA households an encrypted deadline vault and family-readiness plan.
ideas.customer: Households whose work authorization depends on renewable USCIS documents: H-4/L-2 spouses with EADs, F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students, asylum applicants, DACA recipients, and pending adjustment applicants. Sold at $20/mo per household, or $4-8 per head through employers, university international offices, credit unions and churches.
ideas.problem: DHS ended automatic 540-day EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after 30 October 2025. USCIS advises filing up to 180 days early, yet some I-765 categories are reported at many months to a year or more, so gaps in work authorization mean lost jobs, licenses and health coverage. Rich families' lawyers prevent this by tracking every date; ordinary families rely on memory and WhatsApp.
ideas.solution: An end-to-end-encrypted vault, on-device where possible: photograph an EAD, I-94 or I-797 and it extracts dates and builds a household calendar (EAD file window opening at day 180, AR-11 address change within 10 days, OPT unemployment day counter, I-751, N-400 windows, passport expiries). It pre-fills renewal packets for attorney review, generates employer bridging letters, and monitors case status. For cases outside normal processing times it prepares a congressional-inquiry package. It adds a family-readiness plan (power of attorney, standby guardianship for children, contact tree, know-your-rights card). Flat-fee referrals go to attorneys and DOJ-accredited representatives. It is software and documents, not legal advice.
ideas.why_now: The October 2025 interim final rule ended automatic extensions, processing times are long, USCIS moved to a new I-765 form version (mandatory from March 2026), and enforcement anxiety is high in 2026. Employers and universities are scrambling to protect workers.
ideas.revenue_model: $20/mo per household; $3-6 per employee per month for employer or university dashboards; flat referral fees from partner attorneys; enterprise HR reporting tier.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Wealthy people's immigration counsel adds most of its value before a crisis, by calendaring, filing early and pre-drafting backups, which software can supply for a fraction of the cost. Privacy-by-design (end-to-end encryption so a subpoena or breach yields nothing) is not just compliance but the differentiator for a population that fears data exposure. The paying wedge is the professional H-4/OPT segment and their employers, not the most vulnerable households.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a WhatsApp and spreadsheet MVP that ingests document photos and sends reminders. Partner with 2 immigration attorneys on flat-fee referral, 3 university international offices, and H-4 spouse and OPT Facebook groups. Enroll 100 households free, convert to $20/mo, and pilot with one employer HR team.

ideas.title: Findings Sentinel: A Nurse Tracks Your Scan Follow-Ups
ideas.one_liner: What a concierge doctor really sells is closed loops: someone reads every report and owns the follow-up; for $20/mo, a nurse-in-the-loop sentinel makes sure your incidental scan findings do not fall through the cracks.
ideas.customer: Adults 50-80 (and their adult children) who had a CT, MRI, ultrasound or pathology in the last three years. Incidentals include lung nodules, thyroid, adrenal and kidney lesions, pancreatic cysts and aneurysms. Secondary buyers are self-insured employers, Medicare Advantage plans and imaging centers that carry follow-up liability.
ideas.problem: Studies of incidental findings report follow-up failure rates commonly in the 30-60% range (lung nodules especially). The ordering physician is often not notified beyond the report, the PCP is not copied, and under the Cures Act patients see results in portals before anyone explains them. A concierge doctor reads everything and calls; everyone else gets an unread PDF.
ideas.solution: Pull records through patient-directed access (Medicare App Library apps, Apple Health Records, portals) or PDF upload. An LLM extracts each 'recommend follow-up in X months' statement and tracks whether it happened. An RN or NP reviews flagged items and issues a plain-language one-pager with the question to ask and a drafted message or referral request to the PCP. A monthly digest and annual records reconciliation are included. No diagnosis or prescribing, so it is navigation, not telemedicine.
ideas.why_now: CMS's Health Tech Ecosystem launched its Medicare App Library in April 2026 with hundreds of organizations pledged to FHIR-based sharing, and TEFCA-style patient access is maturing. LLMs are reliable at extracting follow-up recommendations from radiology text, the same technique hospital nodule programs use. That makes nurse minutes rare and targeted.
ideas.revenue_model: $20/mo membership; $99 one-time 'catch-up review' of the last three years; $2-4 per member per month from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; imaging centers pay for closed-loop follow-up as risk reduction. Rough cost basis: extraction costs pennies and, if about 8% of members are flagged yearly at about 25 nurse minutes, clinical labor is only a few dollars per member per year.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The concierge doctor's value is not the 60-minute visit; it is that a competent person reads every report and owns the loop. Loop closure is an insurance-like utilization problem: about 95% of members have nothing to flag most months, so the pooled cost fits $20/mo. Immediate-release results created a new market for 'someone to tell me what this means and what happens next'.
ideas.first_30_days: Manually pilot with 30 volunteers recruited from incidentaloma communities and senior centers. Members upload reports, a contract RN reviews them, and you count unclosed loops. Publish the results ('X% had an unclosed loop') for PR, and use them to sign one imaging center or employer pilot before building the app.

ideas.title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
ideas.one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
ideas.customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
ideas.problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
ideas.solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
ideas.why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
ideas.revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.

ideas.title: Scam Fire Drills: A Security Detail for Grandparents
ideas.one_liner: Wealthy families run kidnap and extortion protocols with duress words and a 24/7 first-response team; for $20/mo, give ordinary families rehearsed scam drills and a 15-minute fraud hotline, funded partly by the banks that eat the losses.
ideas.customer: Adult children (35-55) with parents 70+, and the credit unions and community banks that sponsor the service for older members. The buyer pays $20/mo per family, or a bank pays $3-6 per enrolled member.
ideas.problem: FTC data shows consumers reported $15.9B in fraud losses in 2025, with people 50+ reporting $4.3B and impersonation scams over $3.5B. Awareness campaigns fail because panic overrides knowledge in the moment, and identity-monitoring products act after the money is gone. Recovery windows (wire recalls, gift-card and crypto-ATM freezes, ACH returns) are hours long, and most victims do not know the first-hour steps.
ideas.solution: Family onboarding: credit freezes for all members, passkeys and a password manager, SIM-swap locks, a family safe word, and trusted-contact registration at banks. Quarterly consented drills: a scripted call using a synthetic voice (never a relative's cloned voice) tests how the parent responds to a 'grandchild in jail' or 'bank fraud department' scenario, with coaching afterward. A 24/7 hotline answers within 15 minutes with a step-by-step recovery playbook, initiating wire recall, card dispute and gift-card issuer calls while the money can still be clawed back.
ideas.why_now: AI voice cloning has made grandparent and executive-impersonation scams cheap, and 2025 losses jumped by a quarter or more from 2024. Credit unions are actively seeking member-protection programs; for example, Illinois law from 1 January 2026 lets credit union staff contact a member's listed trusted person when exploitation is suspected.
ideas.revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $3-6 per member per month from credit unions and community banks (reduced fraud losses and liability, and a retention benefit); referral fees on identity-theft insurance and data-broker removal partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rehearsal, not awareness, changes behavior under panic, exactly as fire drills do; nobody sells consented scam simulations to families. The first-hour response is where dollars are actually saved, so a human hotline is the product, and the party with the strongest incentive to pay is the financial institution that absorbs the loss.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 20 families through parent-of-aging-parents communities and run a manual onboarding call plus one drill each with a contract fraud analyst on call. Record the drill failure rate as a headline stat. Pitch two local credit unions on a 100-member sponsored pilot, priced at $4 per member per month.

ideas.title: Lifeboat for Students of Closing Colleges
ideas.one_liner: A transfer-rescue service that maps every credit of a closing college's students into a receiving school's degree requirements, paid flat-fee by institutions and states, free to students.
ideas.customer: Payers: closing or distressed private colleges (which must file teach-out plans), state higher-ed agencies and accreditors, and regional receiving colleges that want transfer enrollment. Users: students at the closing school, roughly 500 to 3,000 per small college.
ideas.problem: When a small college closes, teach-out deals are improvised. Nursing, education and arts credits often fail to map. Students face a murky choice, because entering a teach-out forfeits closed-school loan discharge. Transcripts become hard to get, and many students simply stop out. One tally counts nine college closures in 2026, and Philadelphia Fed modeling points to dozens more.
ideas.solution: Within a week of an announced closure, ingest the catalog, syllabi and transcripts into a credit-mapping engine and produce course-by-course equivalency offers from 3 to 5 receiving schools. Give each student a lifeboat file: credits accepted, remaining requirements, time to degree, net price, and the teach-out versus transfer versus loan-discharge tradeoff, in plain language. Add written articulation letters from receiving schools, warm handoffs to admissions, and transcript custody. Offer a paid advocacy tier for credit-denial appeals.
ideas.why_now: The US high-school graduating class peaked in 2025 (about 3.9M) and shrinks about 13% by 2041, so the tuition-dependent-college shakeout is just starting. LLMs can now match syllabi to course equivalencies in hours, work that used to take registrars weeks per student. Receiving schools are hungry for transfer enrollment and closing schools have no bandwidth.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fees only: a closure-response engagement ($25k to $75k) paid by the closing school, its state agency or a consortium; an annual credit-mapping and closure-readiness subscription ($30k to $100k) from receiving colleges; and a $149 to $299 student advocacy add-on. Do not charge per enrolled student, because the Higher Education Act's incentive-compensation ban prohibits enrollment bounties at Title IV schools (confirm with counsel).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Students at a closing college are the highest-intent, highest-credit leads in higher education, but the bounty model that would normally monetize them is illegal, so the business must be paid for labor and neutrality instead. The moat is a growing corpus of verified course equivalencies plus being the trusted neutral on day one of a closure. Accreditors and state agencies need a vendor for teach-out compliance and do not want to be seen picking winners among rival colleges.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a tracker of announced and at-risk closures from accreditor notices and news. Pick the two nearest announced closures and offer their registrars and the state higher-ed agency a free pilot for one program (nursing or education). Line up 3 nearby receiving colleges' transfer directors. Hand-run LLM-assisted credit mapping on 50 students with a contract registrar reviewing, and deliver personal lifeboat files. Close the first flat-fee pilot with a receiving college or state agency, and publish a 'What to do when your college closes' guide for inbound.

ideas.title: Safe-Deposit Box Successor With Heir Protocol
ideas.one_liner: A bonded, insured vault subscription for original wills, deeds, titles, seed-phrase backups and heirlooms, with a scripted release protocol for heirs, sold through estate attorneys as the bank box disappears.
ideas.customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys as the channel, and their clients aged 55 to 85 whose plan says 'the original is in the safe deposit box'. Secondary: coin, gold and crypto holders, and small landlords and business owners holding original deeds and titles.
ideas.problem: Chase said in August 2025 that it would phase out all remaining safe deposit boxes nationwide, after it stopped new rentals in 2021. Capital One, Santander and Citizens exited earlier, and the total number of boxes has reportedly fallen from about 40M to an estimated 25M to 32M. Contents are not FDIC-insured, and no federal law governs boxes. On a death the bank typically freezes access until paperwork clears. The box was the default chain of custody for the paper that proves who owns what, and nothing has replaced it.
ideas.solution: Rent standardized boxes or sealed envelopes inside licensed, bonded vault partners. Each item gets a photo and hash inventory, and contents are insured under a valuables policy. The core product is a designated-heir protocol: on a death certificate plus an attorney letter or executor's letters, the vault releases to the named person after video attestation and dual control. Add periodic proof-of-life check-ins, an index the attorney can see, and an original-will custody service tied to the attorney's office.
ideas.why_now: Chase's nationwide phase-out (announced August 2025) removed the largest holder of boxes. The Great Wealth Transfer is under way. Retail gold and crypto holdings create new 'irreplaceable original' items such as seed backups and coins that people do not want in a home closet.
ideas.revenue_model: $15 to $35 per month per box, or $199 to $399 per year. A $99 onboarding and inventory fee. A $250 heir-release fee. A white-label or referral share of $5 to $10 per client per month for law firms. Margin on the insurance premium.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The box was never about valuables. It was legal chain of custody for original paper, and banks are quitting because vault space is expensive real estate, not because the need went away. The product is the death protocol that banks never offered, since banks freeze access and a vault plus an attorney workflow can release to the named heir within days. Attorneys are the distribution because they carry malpractice risk when originals are lost.
ideas.first_30_days: Check whether your state regulates safe-deposit companies, then sign a white-label deal with one existing bonded vault or secure records-storage operator in a single metro. Draft the release protocol and client agreement with two estate attorneys. Present to 5 estate-planning firms and one senior center with a free 'Where are your originals?' inventory worksheet as the lead magnet. Sell 30 founding-member boxes at a discounted annual rate and run the first two mock heir releases to prove the protocol.

ideas.title: Birth Plan B for Maternity Deserts
ideas.one_liner: Carve the last three weeks of childbirth logistics out of the hospital: pre-booked lodging, ride dispatch, nurse triage and an emergency-delivery kit for mothers whose local labor ward closed.
ideas.customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans and state programs spending Rural Health Transformation money, rural employers and self-insured plans, and mothers directly ($349 to $699). Users: pregnant women in maternity-desert counties.
ideas.problem: At least 96 hospital labor-and-delivery units closed across 35 states between 2024 and early 2026, and in nearly 60% of affected counties it was the only birthing facility. About one in three US counties is a maternity-care desert, and more Medicaid cuts starting in 2027 are expected to close more units. Families improvise the final weeks: a 60 to 90 minute drive, no place to stay at 39 weeks, a partner who cannot leave work, and unplanned roadside births.
ideas.solution: A subscription from week 34. It includes choosing and pre-registering a receiving hospital, plus a contracted hotel or extended-stay room within 15 minutes of that hospital, for the 38 to 41 week window or triggered at first contractions. It adds on-call ride dispatch through a local non-emergency medical transport or taxi operator, with backup childcare and pet care. A 24/7 OB-nurse triage line (a telehealth partner) decides between go now and wait. The kit includes emergency-birth supplies and a 45-minute partner class coordinated with local EMS, and it ends with a return ride and first-week check-ins. No clinical license is needed because it wraps logistics around existing care.
ideas.why_now: CMS awarded the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program to all 50 states on December 29, 2025 (about $200M per state in year one). 35 state applications include maternal or child health, several include obstetric transport, and states face an October 30, 2026 deadline to obligate first-year awards. That makes subcontractors with a concrete pilot unusually welcome right now.
ideas.revenue_model: A per-member-per-pregnancy fee of roughly $300 to $900 from Medicaid managed-care plans as a value-added benefit, or a state RHTP subaward. Consumer self-pay of $349 to $699. Employer add-on for rural self-insured plans. Margin on lodging and rides.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When a unit closes, the hospital's cost disappears and the family's cost explodes in the final three weeks. The fix is logistics (room blocks, dispatch, triage), which a non-clinical startup can assemble in weeks. Medicaid finances roughly four in ten US births and already pays for non-emergency transport, so the payer exists. The wedge is packaging this as a contractable benefit plans can add, with roadside-birth and ED-bypass metrics as proof.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one closure county in the news and its receiving hospital 45 to 90 minutes away. Contract 6 discounted extended-stay rooms, one local transport operator and a telehealth OB-nurse line. Pilot with 20 mothers via the county health department, WIC and rural clinics, priced at cost or free. Log outcomes. Pitch two Medicaid plans' value-added-benefit teams and the state RHTP office with the pilot data and a one-page subaward proposal before the October 30 obligation deadline. In parallel, sell the consumer version through rural parenting groups, churches and doulas.

ideas.title: Year-Three Warranty Claims Agent and Failure Index
ideas.one_liner: An agent that files manufacturer, retailer and credit-card extended-warranty claims when your stuff dies, paid on success, whose claims data becomes a durability index that Amazon's star ratings cannot provide.
ideas.customer: Consumers who bought $200 to $3,000 durables (appliances, e-bikes, laptops, mattresses, power tools) in the past 1 to 4 years. Later data buyers: home-warranty and insurance firms, retailers, brand quality teams and AI shopping agents.
ideas.problem: Amazon's incentives end at the return window, and reviews freeze at week two, but failures happen in year two to four. The money left behind sits in three layers: manufacturer warranties, retailer protection plans and credit-card extended warranty. It goes unclaimed because people cannot find the receipt, do not know which layer applies, or quit at the phone tree. Meanwhile shoppers have no independent durability signal, and the one consumer tool for spotting fake reviews, Fakespot, was shut down by Mozilla in July 2025 for lack of a business model.
ideas.solution: The consumer connects a receipt source (read-only, receipts only, opt-in) and the agent builds a coverage ledger for big purchases: warranty end dates, card-benefit eligibility, retailer plan status. When the user texts that the dishwasher died, the agent assembles the claim packet (receipt, serial number, photos, symptom), files with the right layer over email, chat or a voice agent, and chases it to resolution. Every outcome (brand, model, failure mode, age at failure) goes into an anonymized Failure Index.
ideas.why_now: LLM agents can now read messy receipts and run multi-channel claims at a cost per claim low enough for a success-fee model. AI shopping assistants and agentic checkout need trustworthy durability signals, which star ratings do not supply. Fakespot's 2025 shutdown proved consumers will not pay to check reviews, so the payer has to be the claim recovery itself.
ideas.revenue_model: A success fee of 20% to 25% of recovered value (refund, repair or replacement), or $19 flat per filed claim. In year two, license the Failure Index by API or report to warranty administrators, insurers, retailers and shopping agents ($2k to $25k per month). Affiliate referrals for a better replacement at the moment of failure.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The unowned moment in commerce is month 25, not the purchase. Every incumbent (Amazon, brands, card issuers) profits when claiming is hard, and a failure someone bothered to claim is a labeled ground-truth data point, unlike a star rating. Sell claims recovery to consumers, who will pay, and the byproduct dataset is what the institutions that price durability will pay for.
ideas.first_30_days: Run it concierge-style. Put up a landing page: 'Did your appliance, e-bike or laptop die within 3 years? We file the claim, you pay only if we recover.' Recruit 30 claimants from Reddit (r/appliances, r/ebikes) and local Facebook groups. Draft claims with an LLM and send them by hand, logging every outcome. Pick one category (for example e-bike batteries or robot vacuums) and publish five public posts on what the claims data shows. Approach one home-warranty or appliance-retail company for a paid data pilot.

ideas.title: Rent Renewal Desk for Small Tenants
ideas.one_liner: Contingency-fee lease-renewal negotiation for tenants under 5,000 square feet, armed with the comps and lease abstraction that landlords get from CoStar-class data and small tenants never see.
ideas.customer: Independent restaurants, salons, clinics, small offices and shops with leases expiring in 6 to 18 months. Channels: bookkeepers and CPAs, POS providers and merchant associations.
ideas.problem: Landlords and their brokers negotiate with professional comps and lease abstracts, while small tenants negotiate blind. Tenant-rep brokers skip small deals because the commission is too small, so owners accept the renewal escalator, the personal guarantee and CAM charges by default. Crowdsourced comp platforms such as CompStak sell to brokers and investors, not to a florist with a lease renewal.
ideas.solution: The tenant uploads the lease and the last 12 months of CAM invoices. The desk builds a comp set (public deeds, listing asking rents, pooled tenant-contributed leases, licensed broker data), then returns a one-page 'you pay X% over or under market' report plus a negotiation script and draft letter. An optional we-negotiate tier uses a licensed broker partner, and a CAM audit is an upsell. Renewal alerts fire 18 months before expiry.
ideas.why_now: LLM document extraction can now abstract a 60-page lease and CAM reconciliation in minutes at a cost of cents, work that used to cost a lawyer $500 to $1,500. Tariff and wage pressure has made rent the last fixed cost small operators can still attack. CompStak's give-to-get model shows lease data can be crowdsourced when contributors get something back.
ideas.revenue_model: A $149 fair-rent report. 20% to 25% of first-year rent savings for full negotiation. 25% contingency on CAM overcharges recovered. Bookkeeper and association referral revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry is total at the small end, and the professionals who could close it are priced out by deal size. AI cuts the cost of a competent negotiation to a few hours. The lasting moat is a pooled, tenant-owned lease database, because landlords' data is proprietary but tenants' data is scattered and freely contributed if they get their own comps back.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer a free fair-rent check to 50 businesses in one dense commercial corridor through two local bookkeepers and a merchants' association. Build the lease-abstraction pipeline and a first comp set from the leases collected. Close five contingency negotiations, measure realized savings, and use the results as the sales deck for the next 100 tenants.

ideas.title: Keep-the-House Buyout Desk for Divorcing Spouses
ideas.one_liner: A divorce-specific mortgage desk that keeps the low-rate first mortgage alive, gets the leaving spouse released, and funds the equity buyout with a small second lien instead of a full high-rate cash-out refinance.
ideas.customer: Divorcing homeowners, mostly aged 40 to 65, who want to keep the house. Channels: mediators, divorce attorneys, CDFAs and DIY-divorce platforms.
ideas.problem: A divorce decree cannot release a co-borrower from the mortgage. Only a formal assumption with release, which requires servicer underwriting of the keeping spouse, or a refinance can do that. Many conventional loans are not assumable, though a transfer to a spouse under a decree is exempt from due-on-sale, while FHA, VA and USDA loans can be assumed. Servicers often mishandle these requests. Many homeowners hold first mortgages far below today's rates, so a full refinance wrecks affordability and the house gets sold.
ideas.solution: Intake on loan type, rate, equity and incomes, then a one-page keep versus sell versus refinance model showing blended-rate math. Then execute the sequence: title transfer under the divorce exemption, an assumption-with-release packet built for the servicer, buyout financing through a partner HELOC or closed-end second lien (or a shared-equity note from the leaving spouse), and suggested decree language for attorneys, such as a buyout-financing contingency and a release deadline.
ideas.why_now: Millions of borrowers still hold sub-4% mortgages while current rates are higher, and tappable home equity is large. The share of divorces involving people over 50 keeps growing, and those couples have the most equity. DIY-divorce platforms now produce decrees with no mortgage plan.
ideas.revenue_model: A flat $495 to $995 planning fee. Broker compensation of about 1% to 2% on second-lien or HELOC originations (requires an NMLS-licensed loan officer or partner). Licensing to DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Avoid referral fees to attorneys because of fee-splitting rules.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Lawyers treat the house as a property-division problem when it is a loan-portability problem. The low-rate first mortgage is often the most valuable asset in the marriage. Illustratively, keeping $300k at 3% and borrowing $100k at 8.5% blends to about 4.4%, versus about 6.5% on a $400k cash-out refinance, roughly $300 to $400 a month less in payment. Nobody in the divorce process is paid to run that comparison.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one NMLS-licensed loan officer and two HELOC or second-lien lenders. Publish the calculator and a 'divorce and your mortgage' guide. Offer 5 mediators, divorce attorneys or CDFAs a free house model for their next 10 clients. Process 5 live cases and build servicer-by-servicer playbooks on assumption timelines and release requirements. Then sell the flat-fee plan to DIY-divorce customers.

ideas.title: Last Day Co: Small Business Wind-Down
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee retirement service for owners who do not want to sell, just stop: legal wind-down, lease exit, records custody, customer-list handoff and a proper last day.
ideas.customer: Retiring owners of solo and micro businesses with $100k to $2M in revenue. Start with regulated solo practices (therapists, small medical or dental practices, solo attorneys, CPAs) where closing duties create urgency, then salons, restaurants and contractors.
ideas.problem: McKinsey estimates baby boomers run as many as 6M small and midsize US businesses, with roughly 2.3M to 3M expected to transition ownership this decade, yet only about 54% of owners have a succession plan and about a third of owners over 50 say they cannot find a buyer. Brokers are paid only on sales and skip tiny firms, so most simply shut. That leaves leases, personal guarantees, client records, final payroll and taxes, licenses and customers stranded.
ideas.solution: A productized 90-day closure: state and local filings and final taxes through a partner CPA, lease exit negotiation (buyout or assignment, limiting the personal guarantee), equipment and inventory liquidation, and a records-custody service where Last Day Co acts as professional custodian for 7 to 10 years with client notice and a release process. It also brokers the customer list or goodwill to a vetted local competitor, with a fee to the owner. It closes with a last-day package: customer letter, farewell event, staff reference packets.
ideas.why_now: Boomers are now roughly 62 to 80, so closures are rising toward the McKinsey-projected peak. LLMs make state-specific closure checklists, notices and letters cheap to produce accurately. Remote records custody removes the need for a physical archive.
ideas.revenue_model: A $2,500 to $9,000 flat wind-down fee. Records custody at $25 to $75 per month or a prepaid $1,500 for 7 years. A goodwill-handoff success fee of 10% to 20% of what the acquirer pays. A 10% to 15% liquidation commission.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Brokers sell, and nobody closes. Most owners do not want a sale process, they want to stop, so the real product is permission and completion with liability handled. Custodianship for regulated practices is near-zero-churn recurring revenue, and the customer list is the only asset that survives a closure, so a warm handoff to a neighboring competitor is where the money is.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick solo therapists and solo attorneys in one state. With a local attorney and CPA, write the state-specific 'professional will and closure' playbook. Sell the $299 professional will plus closure plan through the state association newsletter and LinkedIn. Do three discounted pilot closures end to end, build a list of local acquirers for goodwill handoffs, and document each step as a repeatable checklist.

ideas.title: Family Continuity Kit for Mixed-Status Households
ideas.one_liner: A done-with-you, notarized emergency-care package (standby guardianship, power of attorney, school and medical authorizations, wallet card and check-in alerts) for parents who could be detained without notice.
ideas.customer: Immigrant parents in mixed-status families, reached through trusted messengers such as churches, consulates, unions, clinics and schools. Co-payers: cities, counties and foundations funding preparedness, and employers in agriculture, meatpacking and hospitality. Price $49 to $149 per family, sliding scale.
ideas.problem: ICE issued Directive 11064.4 in July 2025 telling officers not to unnecessarily infringe parents' rights, but children still land in limbo when a parent is detained. The legal tools (standby guardianship, power of attorney, medical consent) are known, and nonprofits such as CLINIC and ILRC publish free guides. Execution is the bottleneck: state-specific forms, two-parent signatures, witnesses, a notary, and getting copies to the right person. California updated its guardianship rules in 2026, and city offices such as Chicago's 40th Ward publish emergency-plan guidance, which shows demand.
ideas.solution: A Spanish-first, WhatsApp-friendly workflow that interviews the parent, auto-fills the state's forms, and completes them through remote online notarization or notary-and-witness events at churches and clinics. Each family gets a wallet card with a QR code giving the designated caregiver instant access to the documents, plus school, bank and medical authorizations. Optional check-in alerts notify the caregiver and a legal-aid hotline if a parent misses a check-in. A caregiver checklist explains the first 72 hours. The forms are reviewed by legal-aid partners, and the app never collects immigration status.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement is at historically high levels in 2025 to 2026, and local governments are publishing family preparedness plans and updating guardianship law. Remote online notarization is available in most states, and messaging-app workflows reach families where they already are. Municipal and foundation budgets for know-your-rights work exist now.
ideas.revenue_model: $49 to $149 per family on a sliding scale. Municipal and county contracts to buy kits for residents ($25 to $40 each). Foundation grants. Union or employer benefit at about $5 per employee per year. Licensing to legal-aid organizations that lack completion capacity.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For many immigrant families the highest-consequence legal document is not about immigration at all. It is a twenty-minute notarized form that keeps a child out of the foster system. Free guides exist but completion is low because the burden is witnesses, notaries, state variations and sharing, which can be productized. Payers exist beyond the family, since cities and foundations would rather fund kits than emergency foster placements.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear standby-guardianship statute. Have a legal-aid organization review the forms to avoid unauthorized-practice-of-law problems. Run notary-and-witness events at three churches or clinics and measure cost per completed family. Build the Spanish WhatsApp flow and printed wallet card, and design privacy so nothing about status is stored. Pitch one alderman's or county commissioner's office for a paid pilot of 500 kits.

ideas.title: The Second Ceremony After Direct Cremation
ideas.one_liner: A scattering-day and celebration-of-life concierge for the majority of families who chose cremation with no service and later realize they need a ritual.
ideas.customer: Adult children aged 40 to 65, two to twelve months after a direct cremation of a parent. Channels: online direct-cremation providers, hospice social workers and estate attorneys.
ideas.problem: The NFDA projects a 63.4% US cremation rate for 2025, rising toward 82% by 2045, and direct cremation ($1,000 to $3,000, no viewing, no service) is the fastest-growing segment. Families later improvise: an urn in a closet, a scattering with unclear legality, a restaurant back room. Funeral homes make nothing on this, and direct-cremation providers do not offer events.
ideas.solution: Fixed-price packages. Scattering day: jurisdiction-specific permit and rule guidance, boat or site scouting, a celebrant, a biodegradable urn, photographer or drone, and a livestream for distant relatives. Celebration of life: venue, catering, an AI-assisted slideshow built from the family's photos, an officiant, a guestbook and thank-you notes. Keepsake add-ons such as glass, vinyl, reef or tree. A planner keyed to 'days since death' nudges families at 30, 60 and 90 days.
ideas.why_now: Direct cremation took off with online price comparison, and the NFDA's 2025 report finds most people (58.3%) have attended a funeral at a non-traditional location. AI makes the slideshow, program and eulogy drafting cheap. Cremation providers are looking for post-sale revenue and a 'what now' answer for customers.
ideas.revenue_model: $900 to $4,500 per event: a $500 to $1,200 coordination fee plus 15% to 25% margin on boats, venues and catering. A 10% to 15% referral share to cremation providers that embed the offer. Annual remembrance add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Direct cremation removed the ceremony from the funeral bundle, and the vacuum reappears months later when the buyer is calmer, has a longer planning horizon and pays for meaning rather than logistics. The unbundled piece is the second funeral, and it can be more profitable than the first because there is no legacy funeral-home cost base.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose a coastal city such as San Diego, Seattle or Boston. Contract two licensed boat charters, three celebrants and a photographer. Write one-page scattering compliance sheets for the local jurisdictions. Interview hospice social workers to find referrals, and offer 10 founding families a $650 scattering-day package. Ask two direct-cremation providers to link the offer from their post-cremation emails, and aim for five events by month three.

ideas.title: The 40 Days: Postpartum Confinement Caregiver Guild
ideas.one_liner: A trained, insured, tradition-certified caregiver guild delivering the 26 to 42 day postpartum confinement (yuesao, sanhujori, cuarentena) to diaspora families whose grandmothers are far away.
ideas.customer: New parents in Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, South Asian, Latino and Middle Eastern communities in dense metros, mostly mothers at 30 to 36 weeks. Secondary payers: extended-family gift funds and employers or health plans looking to reduce postpartum depression.
ideas.problem: Confinement care is widely practiced but supplied through informal agencies and word of mouth. A US yuesao runs about $200 to $400 a day for the standard 26 days, and a 42-day term adds roughly 60%. Quality, safety and worker protections vary widely, agencies rarely serve non-Chinese traditions, and parents without a grandmother nearby are left choosing between exhaustion and a gray-market caregiver.
ideas.solution: Build the guild rather than a marketplace. Recruit experienced caregivers and give them W-2 employment, insurance and background checks, plus training in safe sleep, lactation basics, infection control and postpartum warning signs with an escalation path to the family's OB or midwife. Certify them in specific traditions (menus, do's and don'ts) and match on language and tradition. Sell modular tiers: nights only, meals only, 14, 28 or 42 days. Add a plain-language guide for in-laws and partners.
ideas.why_now: Immigrant-heavy metros have a large unmet pool of families who want the ritual, and grandmothers are harder to bring over given tighter visa and travel rules. Employer-of-record and payroll tools make W-2 caregiver employment easy for a tiny company. Postpartum mental health is a rising priority for employers and health plans.
ideas.revenue_model: $5,500 to $12,000 per family per engagement, at about 30% to 35% gross margin after caregiver pay. Meals-only tier at $35 to $55 a day for faster revenue. Employer or plan subsidy of $1,000 to $2,000 per birth. A gift registry for extended family.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is the trusted caregiver, so the moat is a certified workforce (training, payroll, insurance, safety escalation), not a listing site. Confinement is also the same intervention American medicine now calls the fourth trimester, so obstetric practices can refer to it without endorsing folk claims, and it has been an informal cash market that has never been professionalized.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro with a dense Chinese-American or Korean-American community such as the San Gabriel Valley, Flushing or the Bay Area. Recruit 8 experienced caregivers through WeChat groups and existing agencies. Write a three-day training and safety protocol with a postpartum nurse and lactation consultant. Sign 10 founding families with a service guarantee, and sell a meals-only tier to 50 families for faster revenue. Line up two OB practices or doulas for referrals, and set up employer-of-record payroll.

ideas.title: Robot Bullies: Paid Adversarial Pedestrian Panels
ideas.one_liner: A vetted panel of paid 'difficult humans' who kick, block, crowd and confuse sidewalk robots and humanoids on a controlled test range, so robot makers find their failures before the public does.
ideas.customer: Sidewalk delivery robot operators, humanoid and AMR makers preparing EU conformity files and retail or warehouse pilots, city permit offices that want interaction evidence, and robot insurers. First buyers are the safety or field-ops leads at 20 to 50 mid-size robot companies.
ideas.problem: Robots fail on human behavior, not physics. In 2026 an Uber Eats delivery robot was kicked over in Philadelphia, and robots circled in confusion in Lincoln Park in September. Each robot costs about $2,500 to replace, and the backlash is turning into permit fights. Makers test with polite employees or dummies. Nobody sells honest, repeatable samples of teens, drunks, kids, dog-walkers and wheelchair users behaving badly around a machine.
ideas.solution: A rented lot or closed street block set up as a 'behavior range', with a library of scripted provocations (path blocking, tailgating, encirclement by six teens, camera covering, gentle-force shoves, darting child-sized mannequins, cane and wheelchair users, leashed dogs). Screened, consented, insured participants are paid per session. Cameras and force sensors record everything. The output is a report formatted for conformity files and city permit filings, plus a recurring regression-testing subscription. Later: an anonymized 'Chaos Index' that ranks robot models by how they hold up against human misbehavior.
ideas.why_now: Sidewalk robots are now numerous enough to cause visible backlash, with the Philadelphia kicking incidents and the Lincoln Park swarm video. The EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027. ISO 25785-1, the first safety standard for legged and actively balanced robots, is still a draft, so makers have nothing to test against. Humanoid pilots are starting in warehouses and stores.
ideas.revenue_model: Test days at $8k to $25k per protocol set. Annual regression-testing subscriptions from $120k. Rev share with certification bodies (TUV, UL) on referred test packages. Licensing of anonymized behavior data to simulation and model teams.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not test-track capacity. It is honest human misbehavior at scale, and no simulator or employee panel produces it. The moat is the clinical-trial-style infrastructure: consent forms, insurance, screening and a bench of reliable trouble-makers. Robot makers will pay more for a 16-year-old's creativity than for another simulator.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent a parking lot on weekends. Recruit 30 paid participants from campus job boards at about $30 per hour. Have a lawyer draft consent forms and buy $2M of general liability. Pitch one local sidewalk-robot operator or university warehouse-robot startup a $5k to $10k 'chaos day' with a written report. Publish a free 'Chaos Report' on the Philadelphia-style behaviors to generate inbound leads.

ideas.title: Pay-Per-Decibel Neighbor Trust for Data Centers
ideas.one_liner: An independent trust that owns a sensor mesh around a data center and automatically pays nearby households every time the hum exceeds agreed limits, turning 'trust us' into a self-executing contract.
ideas.customer: Data center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams, their land-use counsel, and counties negotiating community benefit agreements. Pre-application projects facing a rezoning fight are the entry point.
ideas.problem: Local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130B of US data center projects in 2026, and opposition groups more than doubled to 833 by March. Developers' flat checks get called bribes: a $10,000-per-household offer to 4,500 households was rejected by residents in September. Noise promises are unenforceable, and dBA ordinances miss the low-frequency hum residents complain about. Counties lack staff to monitor compliance.
ideas.solution: A neighbor trust, funded by a developer bond, with three parts. (1) Trust-owned acoustic, low-frequency and vibration sensors, publicly viewable in real time. (2) A pre-agreed parametric schedule: any household within the radius gets an automatic payment for each night the level exceeds the threshold, so the payout works like a warranty on quiet. (3) Escalation funding for window and HVAC retrofits if exceedances persist. The trust also reports compliance to the county, giving regulators enforcement without new staff.
ideas.why_now: Opposition is peaking (about 120 projects stalled in H1 2026, more than 300 state bills, moratoria such as New York's), and developers are now experimenting with direct household payments and getting burned on credibility. Developers now need a neutral administrator, and no obvious specialist exists.
ideas.revenue_model: Developer pays $150k to $500k setup per campus, plus 8% to 12% of the annual fund as administration, plus sensor-as-a-service fees. Add county compliance-monitoring contracts. A single multi-billion-dollar campus can absorb this as a rounding error against months of delay.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Neighbors rarely reject data centers over money. They reject unmeasured, unpriced harm. Making the harm measured and self-paying changes the negotiation and gives the developer a real financial reason to buy quieter chillers and dampers. The low-frequency, night-time signature is what the trust measures, and ordinances miss it.
ideas.first_30_days: List the next five county hearings on data center rezoning from local news and Data Center Watch. Hire a freelance acoustic engineer and build a $2k-per-node sensor kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer a free 60-day neutral baseline noise map to one pending project, in front of both the developer and the opposition group. Convert that goodwill into a paid pre-application baseline of $50k to $100k and an MOU for the trust structure.

ideas.title: Smell Graders for Recycled Plastic
ideas.one_liner: A network of trained human noses that gives every batch of post-consumer recycled plastic an odor grade from 1 to 5, creating the price tier and spec that brands need to hit recycled-content mandates.
ideas.customer: Plastic recyclers selling PCR resin (HDPE, PP), converters that mold bottles and tubs, and brand owners in personal care, household and food buying PCR under EU and US recycled-content rules. The recyclers' quality managers buy first, then brand procurement teams.
ideas.problem: Odor is one of the biggest barriers to using recycled plastic. Recyclers can't tell buyers reliably what a batch smells like. Brands reject loads or cap PCR percentages out of caution. Lab methods such as GC-olfactometry are slow and costly, and there's no shared odor grade the way coffee has the Q-score.
ideas.solution: A standard protocol (heated headspace jars, blind triplicates, a reference odor kit, descriptor vocabulary such as rancid, detergent, smoky) run by a panel of trained sniffers recruited from perfumers, coffee Q-graders, sommeliers and food-sensory panelists. Recyclers mail samples and get a 48-hour graded report. Human scores then train an e-nose and GC model that lowers cost per test. Over time it becomes a certification: license and train graders, and publish the grade spec brands cite in purchase contracts.
ideas.why_now: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation applies from 12 August 2026, with 2030 recycled-content minimums (30% for contact-sensitive PET, 10% for other contact-sensitive plastics). Brands have to buy far more PCR within a few years. Sensor vendors need human-panel labels to train on, and none has a standard odor tier to price against.
ideas.revenue_model: $120 to $250 per batch grade. Weekly-lot subscriptions for recyclers. Vendor-qualification programs for brands at $30k or more per year. Grader certification and training fees. Licensing of the labeled dataset to e-nose makers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Regulation mandates recycled content, but a human nose decides whether the resin is usable, and buyers will not trust a grade until someone standardizes it. Whoever owns the grading standard sets the price tiers for the whole PCR market, a bit like coffee's Q-grading. Human panels remain the legal and commercial ground truth even after e-noses arrive.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 12 sniffers from local specialty roasters and perfume or flavor schools. Buy vials, a hot plate and a reference odor kit for under $1,000. Offer three regional recyclers free grading of 20 batches each, and check the grades against their buyers' rejection history. Then price it. Publish a free 'PCR smell atlas' to attract recycler and brand inbound.

ideas.title: Responsible-Charge Network for AI-Made Professional Work
ideas.one_liner: Licensed engineers and architects take legal responsibility for AI-generated permit sets per review, with a review-telemetry audit trail that also lowers malpractice premiums.
ideas.customer: AI-native firms that generate permit drawings, structural letters and MEP plans for ADUs, solar, decks and prefab, and the small design firms that use them. They need licensed sign-off in many states and don't want to employ engineers everywhere.
ideas.problem: AI can draft a permit set in an hour, but only a licensed human can seal it. Startups hire engineers state by state or rely on stamp mills. Regulators and insurers fear rubber-stamping, and 'responsible charge' (the legal standard that the professional actually directed the work) is unprovable. Existing AI-drawing companies such as Spacial keep licensed engineers in-house, so smaller entrants have no good option.
ideas.solution: A vetted network of licensed professionals paid a fixed fee per stamped package, plus software that records how the review happened: time on sheet, checks completed, redlines, overrides. That log becomes the defensible 'responsible-charge' record for state boards, and it underwrites cheaper E&O coverage through an MGA partner. Start narrow with structural and engineering letters for residential ADU, deck and solar permits in three states.
ideas.why_now: AI permit-set generators are moving from demos to real volume, and the standard practice is a licensed engineer reviewing before sealing. Professional liability carriers now ask about AI use, and licensing boards are issuing AI guidance. Nobody has built the shared review-evidence layer.
ideas.revenue_model: 25% to 35% take on engineer fees of $150 to $600 per package. MGA commission on E&O premiums. SaaS fee for the telemetry and audit-trail software.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In AI-delivered professional services, the scarce input is not intelligence but a person who can lose a license. Whoever holds verifiable proof of actual review owns the pricing of liability, which is worth more than the stamps. The product is explicitly anti-stamp-mill: it makes shallow review visible and expensive.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 semi-retired PEs across three states. Sign two AI-permit startups or ADU designers with a backlog. Run the review flow manually with screen recordings and checklists to gather telemetry. Meet one small-firm E&O broker about a pilot rider for reviewed AI work.

ideas.title: Live-In Guardians for Probate Houses
ideas.one_liner: Vetted live-in 'guardians' keep a house occupied while an estate is in probate, so the executor keeps insurance validity, avoids vacancy losses and pays less than for a vacant-home policy.
ideas.customer: Executors, estate and probate attorneys, professional fiduciaries and out-of-state heirs holding an inherited house. Attorneys are the channel, and executors and estates pay.
ideas.problem: Probate sales often take 6 to 12 months or longer. Most homeowners policies limit or exclude coverage after 30 to 60 days of vacancy, so a burst pipe, vandal or squatter can leave the estate uncovered, and specialty vacant-home policies cost far more. The executor is a non-expert with fiduciary liability, often living out of state, and has no one to check the house.
ideas.solution: Place screened guardians (night-shift nurses, travel clinicians, grad students, apprentice tradespeople) in probate houses under a state-specific license agreement rather than a lease. Guardians pay a low monthly fee, keep utilities on, handle mail and lawn, and file daily check-in logs. The estate gets an 'occupied' attestation accepted by a partner insurer or MGA, monthly photo reports, and a house that shows better at sale time. Upsell cleanout and staging at sale.
ideas.why_now: Boomer estates are moving through probate in growing numbers, and homeowners insurers are tightening on nonrenewals and vacancy. Housing costs are high enough that many good tenants will accept a small duty load for below-market housing. UK-style property guardianship exists for commercial buildings, but the US probate house niche is open.
ideas.revenue_model: Estate pays $250 to $500 per month service fee. Guardian pays a program fee. Carrier or MGA commission on the policy. Fees on cleanout, staging and sale-transition services.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The customer isn't buying a house sitter; the estate is buying continued insurance validity and a checklist that satisfies a fiduciary. Occupied status changes the risk class of the asset for the whole probate period. Legal structure (license, not lease, chosen state by state) is the real product and the barrier to copycats.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch 15 probate and estate-planning attorneys in one metro on a pilot for their next three vacant homes. Recruit guardians through hospital and travel-nurse groups. Have a landlord-tenant attorney draft the license and pick a landlord-friendly state to start (for example Texas or Tennessee). Line up a vacant-dwelling insurance broker who will recognize the guardian arrangement. First revenue within about six weeks.

ideas.title: Buy the Restaurant Alley: Used-Oil Route Roll-Up
ideas.one_liner: Consolidate small used-cooking-oil haulers into one AI-run route business, then sell every other mandated back-of-restaurant service from the same truck.
ideas.customer: Independent restaurants and small chains (who now get paid for their oil and buy add-on services), renewable diesel and SAF refiners buying traceable domestic feedstock, and retiring collector owners selling their routes.
ideas.problem: From 2026 the 45Z clean-fuel credit applies only to North American feedstock, and UCO prices have run at roughly $1,000 to $1,400 per tonne. Restaurants historically gave oil away under auto-renewing contracts with big renderers, and theft is common. Small collectors lack chain-of-custody paperwork and contamination grading, and refiners want traceable domestic supply.
ideas.solution: Acquire 8 to 15 small collectors, grease-trap pumpers and hood cleaners in one metro. AI ops: fill-level sensors or photo estimates to cut truck miles 25% to 40%, vision-based contamination grading at pickup, automatic chain-of-custody and sustainability documentation for refiners, and a contract-reading agent that finds competitors' termination windows and times win-back offers. Add hood cleaning, grease-trap pumping and fire-suppression inspection on the same route visits.
ideas.why_now: 45Z limits credits to North American feedstock from 2026, which makes domestic UCO scarce and valuable, and documentation that used to be optional is now a selling point. Owners of small routes are aging out, and route-optimization and photo-grading tools are cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: Spread on oil resale to refiners with a share paid to restaurants, plus $150 to $500 per add-on service visit, plus a traceability premium from refiners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real asset isn't the trucks; it's the contract calendar. Thousands of evergreen grease agreements with 30 to 90 day cancellation windows can be read, mapped and timed. The alley visit is also the cheapest customer touchpoint for every other mandated back-of-house service.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach a retiring one-truck collector about a seller-financed purchase in the $200k to $600k range, or start as a broker with a subcontracted truck offering 20 to 30 restaurants a paid pickup. Build a photo-based intake and contract tracker. Target franchisee groups with 5 to 10 units. Pre-sell forward oil volume to a regional biodiesel or renewable diesel refiner using documented chain of custody.

ideas.title: Roll Up the Layer Under Funeral Homes
ideas.one_liner: Instead of buying funeral homes, buy the removal services and wholesale crematories that independent homes depend on, and run them with AI dispatch, chain-of-custody and paperwork agents.
ideas.customer: Independent funeral homes, roughly 60% to 70% of which have no crematory of their own, plus hospice and medical-examiner contractors. Families are indirect beneficiaries.
ideas.problem: Consolidators are buying the retail funeral homes that families see, and independents are squeezed. Independents struggle to staff 24/7 first-call removals, outsource cremation to small crematories with uneven chain-of-custody, and lose days chasing physician signatures in state electronic death registration systems. Families cannot see where their loved one is.
ideas.solution: Buy regional removal companies and wholesale crematories from retiring owners. AI ops layer: a dispatch agent for 3 a.m. first calls and routing, barcode and photo chain-of-custody at every handoff with a family-facing status link (like package tracking), a paperwork agent that chases physician and ME signatures and files EDRS entries, permits and cremation authorizations, and capacity balancing across retorts. Sell independents a per-case bundle that lets them offer end-to-end service without capital or overnight staff.
ideas.why_now: Independent homes face consolidation pressure and the shift to cremation, and overnight labor is scarce. States are modernizing death-registration workflows (for example Michigan's March 2026 HB 4077 and 4078), and voice and browser agents can now do first-call dispatch and portal filing.
ideas.revenue_model: $150 to $300 per removal, $250 to $450 per wholesale cremation, and $50 to $100 per case for paperwork. A typical home with 150 cases per year yields $60k to $120k of annual revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone is buying the storefront. The stickier profit pools are the invisible utilities behind thousands of small homes, and the hard parts (3 a.m. dispatch, custody proof, signature chasing) are exactly what AI operations do well. Serving independents also positions the roll-up as their ally against consolidators.
ideas.first_30_days: Ride along with one or two removal services. Offer five funeral homes a 'paperwork chaser' that monitors EDRS status and emails doctors, at about $60 per case. Then buy or partner with the removal company serving them, using seller notes. Build the family status link early and let funeral directors show it to families.

ideas.title: Backflow Testers Roll-Up With Portal-Filing Agents
ideas.one_liner: Consolidate small backflow-test shops, then use agents to parse city notices, schedule tests and file results in each water utility's portal, turning mandated annual tests into a low-churn route business.
ideas.customer: Property managers, restaurants, car washes, medical buildings, HOAs and multifamily owners who must test backflow assemblies annually, and water utilities who benefit from compliance. Retiring tester shops are the sellers.
